factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a firm’s change in capital investment intensity relative to the average change observed among firms in the same two-digit industry classification. It follows the spirit of the “RCAPX” style signal in Abarbanell and Bushee (1998) by focusing on growth in capital expenditures and then removing contemporaneous industry-wide movements.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction uses firm identifiers and a monthly availability timestamp, plus annual accounting items for capital expenditures and net property, plant, and equipment. It also uses an industry code that can be truncated to its first two characters to define the industry group used for benchmarking.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the merged firm-month panel that contains the industry code, capital expenditures, and net property, plant, and equipment. Sort observations by firm identifier and the monthly availability timestamp to support time-based lag matching.

Define the industry group by converting the industry code to text and taking its first two characters. This two-character prefix is used as the industry identifier for cross-sectional averaging each month.

Impute missing capital expenditures using the change in net property, plant, and equipment over the prior 12 months. The imputation is $capx_t \leftarrow ppent_t - ppent_{t-12}$ when the original $capx_t$ is missing.

Compute calendar-based lags of capital expenditures at 12 and 24 months prior, matched by the same firm and the timestamp shifted back by 12 or 24 months. Form the two-year reference level as the average of these two lags.

Compute the primary percentage change in capital expenditures relative to the two-year reference average. If the reference average equals zero, set this percentage change to missing to mirror division-by-zero producing missing.

For observations where the primary percentage change is missing, compute a fallback percentage change using only the 12-month lag. If the 12-month lag equals zero, set the fallback to missing.

Within each month and two-digit industry group, compute the cross-sectional mean of the firm-level percentage change. Subtract this industry-month mean from the firm’s percentage change to obtain the industry-adjusted signal.

Drop observations where the final signal is missing. Convert the monthly availability timestamp into an integer year-month key of the form YYYYMM for output.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $t$ denote the monthly availability timestamp, and let $t-12$ and $t-24$ denote the timestamps exactly 12 and 24 months earlier.

If capital expenditures are missing, impute:
$$
capx_t^{*} =
\begin{cases}
capx_t, & \text{if } capx_t \text{ is observed} \\
ppent_t - ppent_{t-12}, & \text{if } capx_t \text{ is missing}
\end{cases}
$$

Define lagged values and the two-lag average:
$$
capx_{t-12}^{*},\; capx_{t-24}^{*}
$$
$$
\overline{capx}_{t} = \frac{1}{2}\left(capx_{t-12}^{*} + capx_{t-24}^{*}\right)
$$

Primary percentage change:
$$
pchcapx_t =
\begin{cases}
\frac{capx_t^{*} - \overline{capx}_{t}}{\overline{capx}_{t}}, & \text{if } \overline{capx}_{t} \neq 0 \\
\text{missing}, & \text{if } \overline{capx}_{t} = 0
\end{cases}
$$

Fallback percentage change when the primary is missing:
$$
pchcapx_t =
\begin{cases}
\frac{capx_t^{*} - capx_{t-12}^{*}}{capx_{t-12}^{*}}, & \text{if } pchcapx_t \text{ is missing and } capx_{t-12}^{*} \neq 0 \\
\text{missing}, & \text{if } pchcapx_t \text{ is missing and } capx_{t-12}^{*} = 0
\end{cases}
$$

Industry-month mean using the two-character industry group $g$:
$$
\mu_{g,t} = \frac{1}{N_{g,t}} \sum_{i \in g} pchcapx_{i,t}
$$

Industry-adjusted change in capital investment:
$$
ChInvIA_{i,t} = pchcapx_{i,t} - \mu_{g,t}
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
All lags are calendar-based, requiring an observation exactly 12 or 24 months earlier; otherwise the lag is missing. If both the two-lag average and the 12-month lag are unusable due to zero denominators or missing lags, the signal is missing and the observation is dropped.

If net property, plant, and equipment is missing at $t$ or $t-12$, then the imputation for missing capital expenditures cannot be formed. In that case, capital expenditures remain missing and the signal will typically be missing.

The industry benchmark is computed using all available firm observations in the same two-character industry group and month with non-missing percentage changes. If an industry-month has only one valid firm, the benchmark equals that firm’s value, producing a zero industry-adjusted signal for that firm.

The timestamp used is the monthly availability date, and the output month key is derived directly from that timestamp. The factor is therefore aligned to when the accounting information is considered available, not necessarily the fiscal period end.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly firm-level signal named ChInvIA. Each record contains a firm identifier, an integer month key in YYYYMM format, and the signal value as a real number. Records with missing signal values are excluded from the output.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Capital expenditures are treated as the primary investment flow measure, with a fallback imputation based on the annual change in net property, plant, and equipment when capital expenditures are missing. Industry adjustment uses a two-digit truncation of the provided industry code, computed as the first two characters after converting the code to text.

factor_logic_in_paper.factor_name: Amihud illiquidity (12-month average of monthly Amihud daily illiquidity)
factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures price impact per unit of trading activity, following Amihud (2002). It summarizes how much absolute return is associated with a given dollar-volume proxy, averaged over the prior twelve months.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction uses a daily trading date, a daily total return, a daily end-of-day price, and a daily share volume. The output is a monthly predictor value labeled as Amihud illiquidity.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, map each daily observation to a monthly availability timestamp in $YYYYMM$ format using the calendar year and month of the trading date.

Next, compute a daily illiquidity statistic as absolute daily return divided by the product of absolute price and share volume. Replace any infinite values from invalid divisions with missing.

Then, aggregate the daily illiquidity statistic to the month by taking the simple average across all trading days in that month for each security. This produces a monthly illiquidity series.

Next, sort the monthly series by security and month, and create eleven monthly lags of the monthly illiquidity value. These lags represent the prior eleven months, alongside the current month.

Then, count how many of the twelve values (current plus eleven lags) are non-missing for each security-month. Compute the twelve-month mean only when all twelve values are present; otherwise set the result to missing.

Finally, label the month field as $YYYYMM$ for the output and drop any rows where the twelve-month illiquidity value is missing. The remaining rows form the final monthly factor file.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Define the monthly timestamp as:
$$
yyyymm = 100 \cdot \text{year}(\text{date}) + \text{month}(\text{date})
$$

Define daily Amihud illiquidity for day $d$ as:
$$
ill_d = \frac{|ret_d|}{|prc_d| \cdot vol_d}
$$
and set $ill_d$ to missing when it is infinite.

Define monthly illiquidity for month $t$ as the mean across trading days in that month:
$$
ill_t = \frac{1}{N_t}\sum_{d \in t} ill_d
$$

Define the reported predictor as the twelve-month mean of the current and prior eleven monthly values:
$$
Illiquidity_t = \frac{1}{12}\sum_{k=0}^{11} ill_{t-k}
$$
computed only if all $ill_{t-k}$ for $k=0,\dots,11$ are non-missing; otherwise $Illiquidity_t$ is missing.
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If price is zero or volume is zero, the daily ratio can become infinite; these infinite values are converted to missing before monthly averaging. Missing daily returns, prices, or volumes propagate to missing daily illiquidity and reduce the number of valid days in the monthly mean.

The twelve-month value is only produced when the current month and each of the prior eleven months have non-missing monthly illiquidity. This is a strict requirement: any missing month in the window forces the twelve-month result to be missing.

The signal is timestamped at the month level using the month derived from the daily trading date. The value for month $t$ uses information from month $t$ and the prior eleven months, as constructed from the available daily data.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel keyed by security identifier and $YYYYMM$ month. It contains a single numeric column equal to the twelve-month illiquidity measure, with all rows having missing values removed.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The daily illiquidity uses absolute price to neutralize signed price conventions. The monthly aggregation is an unweighted mean across trading days, and the twelve-month aggregation is an unweighted mean across months with a complete twelve-month history.

factor_logic_in_paper.factor_name: Quarterly return on assets using a three-month lagged asset base
factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures quarterly operating profitability scaled by the asset base that was observable three months earlier. The intent is to align the income flow for the quarter with a lagged stock measure of assets to reduce look-ahead and timing mismatches.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction requires a master linking table that provides a stable company identifier mapping and the monthly availability timestamp for each firm observation. It also requires quarterly fundamentals containing quarter-end total assets and quarterly income before extraordinary items, each stamped with the same monthly availability timestamp. The final output is a monthly-dated file containing the firm identifier, a year-month key, and the computed signal value.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the master linking table and keep only observations with a valid fundamental-company identifier. Join this filtered master to the quarterly fundamentals on the fundamental-company identifier and the monthly availability timestamp. Keep only rows that match in both sources.

Within each firm, order observations by the monthly availability timestamp. For each observation, create a lagged timestamp equal to the current availability timestamp minus three calendar months. This lagged timestamp defines which prior asset value will be used as the scaling base.

Create a lookup table containing, for each firm and availability timestamp, the quarter-end total assets. Rename its timestamp to the three-month-lag timestamp and rename assets to indicate it is lagged. Merge this lookup back to the main table on firm and the three-month-lag timestamp to obtain lagged assets.

Compute the signal as quarterly income before extraordinary items divided by the three-month-lagged quarter-end total assets. Remove observations where the computed signal is missing. Convert the monthly availability timestamp into an integer year-month key and retain only the firm identifier, year-month key, and signal.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $t$ denote the monthly availability timestamp for an observation, and let $t-3m$ denote the timestamp three calendar months earlier.

Let $IBQ_t$ be quarterly income before extraordinary items available at $t$, and let $ATQ_{t-3m}$ be quarter-end total assets available at $t-3m$ for the same firm.

The factor value is
$$
ROA^{(q)}_t = \frac{IBQ_t}{ATQ_{t-3m}}.
$$

The reported time index is the year-month key
$$
YYYYMM = 100 \cdot \text{year}(t) + \text{month}(t).
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a firm lacks a valid fundamental-company identifier in the master linking table, it is excluded before any merging. If the quarterly fundamentals do not have a matching record for the same identifier and availability month, the observation is dropped by the inner join.

If the three-month-lagged assets record is not found for the firm at $t-3m$, the lagged assets are missing and the factor is missing. Such missing factor values are removed from the output. No special handling is applied for zero or negative lagged assets; the ratio is computed as written when the denominator is present.

The factor is timestamped by the monthly availability month $t$, not by the fiscal quarter-end date. The denominator uses assets from exactly three calendar months prior to $t$, matched on the same firm and availability month.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel with one row per firm-month where the factor is computable. It contains exactly three fields: a firm identifier, an integer year-month key, and the factor value. The factor value is a floating-point ratio equal to quarterly income before extraordinary items divided by three-month-lagged quarter-end total assets.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Total assets at quarter-end are a stock measure and can jump due to restatements or acquisitions, which can create large changes in the denominator. Quarterly income before extraordinary items is a flow measure and may be restated when firms reclassify items, affecting the numerator. The factor is a constructed signal intended for monthly use, derived from quarterly fundamentals aligned to a monthly availability calendar.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures operating profitability on a cash-like basis by adjusting accrual operating profits for working-capital related balance-sheet changes and selected liability changes. It is designed to better reflect operating performance that is closer to cash generation than standard accrual profitability. The final signal is scaled by total assets to improve comparability across firms and over time.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction requires a monthly security-level panel that includes identifiers, availability timing, share-class and industry classification fields, and market equity. It also requires accounting items for revenue, operating expenses, working-capital components, selected debt and accrual liability components, total assets, and common equity. All accounting items are used as of the month they become available in the monthly panel.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the merged monthly panel where each observation corresponds to a firm and a month of information availability. Treat missing values as zero for revenue, cost of goods sold, selling/general/administrative expense, research and development expense, receivables, inventories, prepaid expenses, current debt, long-term debt related to leases/other, accounts payable, and accrued expenses.

Create a calendar-based 12-month lag for each working-capital and liability component used in the adjustments. The lag must match the same firm and the observation whose availability month is exactly 12 months earlier. If no such month exists for the firm, the 12-month lag value is missing.

Compute cash-based operating profitability in levels by taking accrual operating profitability and then subtracting increases in operating current assets and adding increases in selected operating liabilities. Specifically, subtract the 12-month change in receivables, inventories, and prepaid expenses, and add the 12-month change in accounts payable and accrued expenses. Also add the 12-month change in the combined debt components used in the specification.

Scale the resulting level measure by total assets from the same availability month. Separately compute a log book-to-market value using common equity divided by market equity, and use it only to determine whether the observation is eligible.

Apply exclusions by setting the factor to missing when the security fails the share-class screen, has missing market equity, has missing log book-to-market, has missing total assets, or is in the excluded industry range. After exclusions, drop any temporary lagged fields and the temporary book-to-market field, keeping only the factor.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Define accrual operating profitability with an explicit research and development adjustment as
$$
OP = \text{Revenue} - \text{Cost of goods sold} - (\text{SG\&A} - \text{R\&D}).
$$

Define 12-month calendar changes for any balance-sheet item $X$ as
$$
\Delta_{12} X = X_t - X_{t-12},
$$
where $t-12$ refers to the observation with the same firm and an availability month exactly 12 months earlier.

Define the cash-based operating profitability numerator as
$$
CBOP^{num} = OP - \Delta_{12}\text{Receivables} - \Delta_{12}\text{Inventories} - \Delta_{12}\text{Prepaids}
+ \Delta_{12}\text{Accounts payable} + \Delta_{12}\text{Accrued expenses}
+ \Delta_{12}\text{Debt components},
$$
with
$$
\Delta_{12}\text{Debt components} = (\text{Current debt} + \text{Long-term lease/other debt})_t - (\text{Current debt} + \text{Long-term lease/other debt})_{t-12}.
$$

Scale by total assets to obtain the final factor value:
$$
CBOperProf_t = \frac{CBOP^{num}}{\text{Total assets}_t}.
$$

Compute the temporary log book-to-market used for filtering as
$$
BM_t = \log\left(\frac{\text{Common equity}_t}{\text{Market equity}_t}\right).
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
Calendar-based lagging is required: the 12-month lag uses the same firm and the month exactly 12 months earlier, not the prior row. If the exact 12-month earlier observation is absent, the lagged value is missing and the factor will typically become missing through arithmetic propagation.

Zero-filling is applied only to the specified operating flow and balance-sheet components used in the numerator adjustments. Total assets, common equity, and market equity are not zero-filled; missing values in these fields can invalidate the observation.

Scaling by total assets requires non-missing total assets; if total assets is missing, the factor is set to missing by the exclusion rule. If total assets is zero, the division yields an undefined or infinite value; such cases should be treated as invalid and effectively missing.

The book-to-market term is used only as an eligibility check; the factor output does not include it. If common equity or market equity makes the log undefined (for example, non-positive ratio), the resulting missing value triggers exclusion.

Industry exclusion removes firms with classification codes in the financial range from 6000 inclusive to 7000 exclusive. The share-class exclusion removes securities with share codes greater than 11.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a single monthly predictor series named CBOperProf at the firm-security level, aligned to the month of information availability. Values are real numbers representing cash-based operating profitability scaled by total assets, with ineligible observations set to missing. The output contains no auxiliary columns used for lagging or filtering.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Revenue is total operating revenue, cost of goods sold is direct production cost, and SG&A is operating overhead; research and development is subtracted from SG&A to avoid double-counting when R&D is separately reported. Receivables, inventories, and prepaid expenses proxy for operating current assets whose increases typically consume cash, so their increases reduce the cash-based measure. Accounts payable and accrued expenses proxy for operating liabilities whose increases typically provide financing, so their increases raise the cash-based measure. The debt-component change term follows the provided implementation and is treated as an additive adjustment based on the specified debt items.

factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a monthly security identifier, a monthly availability timestamp, and a monthly market value of equity at the share-class level. The market value of equity is the stock-level market capitalization measure built from price and shares outstanding, with units depending on the upstream convention.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the monthly master table containing the security identifier, the monthly availability timestamp, and the market value of equity. Compute the size signal as the natural logarithm of the market value of equity.

Remove observations where the computed size signal is missing. This ensures the output contains only valid numeric size values.

Convert the monthly availability timestamp into an integer year-month key. The key is formed as $100 \times \text{year} + \text{month}$.

Keep only the security identifier, the year-month key, and the size signal. Output the resulting monthly panel in that column order.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures how large a firm’s sales are relative to its equity market value. It operationalizes the sales-to-price ratio used in Barbee, Mukherji, and Raines (1996), Table 2, model 1.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a monthly-availability timestamp, a sales (net) measure from financial statements, and a firm-level market equity measure aggregated across share classes. Sales are defined as net sales of goods and services after returns and allowances, reported as an annual flow in millions of USD. Market equity is the firm-level market capitalization in the same currency scale, aggregated at the firm level by summing market caps across linked share classes for that month.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the sales input keyed by security identifier and monthly availability timestamp. If multiple sales records exist for the same identifier and timestamp, keep the first record.

Join the sales data to the firm-level market equity data using an inner join on the same identifier and monthly availability timestamp. This restricts the sample to observations where both sales and market equity are present at that timestamp.

Compute sales-to-price as sales divided by firm-level market equity. Then drop observations where the computed ratio is missing.

Convert the monthly availability timestamp to an integer year-month key $yyyymm$ using calendar year and month. Keep only the identifier, $yyyymm$, and the computed sales-to-price value, and write the result to a CSV.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
The signal is computed as:
$$
SP_{i,t}=\frac{Sales_{i,t}}{MVE_{i,t}}
$$

The year-month output key is computed from the availability date as:
$$
yyyymm = 100 \times year(time\_avail\_m) + month(time\_avail\_m)
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If sales or market equity is missing at the monthly availability timestamp, the observation is excluded because the join requires both fields. If the computed ratio is missing after division, it is dropped.

If market equity is zero, the division yields an undefined or infinite value depending on the system; the implementation only explicitly removes missing values, not infinities. Users should be aware that extremely small market equity can create extreme ratios.

Sales are an annual flow but are used at the monthly availability timestamp provided by the input. The factor therefore reflects the most recently available sales figure as of that monthly timestamp, without additional lag logic beyond the provided availability date.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract:
The output is a CSV containing one row per security identifier and year-month key where both inputs are available. The columns are the security identifier, $yyyymm$, and $SP$.

$SP$ is a unitless ratio formed from sales and market equity expressed in consistent currency units. The output frequency is monthly, indexed by $yyyymm$ derived from the availability timestamp.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Sales (net) represents net sales of goods and services after returns and allowances and is commonly used as a revenue proxy, though definitions can vary when non-operating revenues are material. Firm-level market equity aggregates market capitalization across all share classes linked to the same firm, which improves comparability when multiple share classes exist.

factor_logic_in_paper.factor_name: Earnings-to-Price Ratio with a six-month market value lag
factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures profitability relative to market valuation by scaling income before extraordinary items by a market equity value observed exactly six calendar months earlier. The six-month lag is intended to align accounting information with a plausibly investable price base and reduce look-ahead concerns.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses income before extraordinary items and a firm-level market equity measure that aggregates market capitalization across share classes at the firm level. The income measure is an annual flow variable, while the market equity measure is monthly and is used with a six-month calendar lag. The output is a monthly signal keyed by an identifier and a year-month timestamp.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, for each security identifier and month, retain a single income observation by taking the first available record within that month. Then join the monthly market equity data with the monthly income data on the same identifier and month.

Next, order observations by identifier and month to support calendar-based lag alignment. Create a new month field equal to the current month minus six calendar months.

Then construct a lag table that maps each identifier and month to that month’s market equity value. Rename the month in this lag table to the six-month-lag month field, and rename market equity to indicate it is lagged.

Merge the main table with the lag table on identifier and the six-month-lag month field. This attaches the market equity from exactly six calendar months earlier when that earlier month exists in the data.

Compute the earnings-to-price ratio as income before extraordinary items divided by the six-month-lagged market equity. Set the ratio to missing when it is negative, and then drop all rows where the ratio is missing.

Finally, convert the month timestamp into an integer year-month format and keep only the identifier, year-month, and the computed ratio. Write the resulting monthly panel to the specified output file.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
For a given firm-identifier $i$ and month $t$, define the six-month calendar lag month as $t-6$.

The factor value is
$$
EP_{i,t}=\frac{IB_{i,t}}{MVE_{i,t-6}}.
$$

The published value applies the filter
$$
EP_{i,t} \leftarrow \text{missing if } EP_{i,t}<0,
$$
and then removes missing values from the output.
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If the six-month-lagged month $t-6$ is not present for the identifier, the lagged market equity is missing and the factor is dropped. If income is missing at month $t$, the ratio is missing and the observation is dropped.

If lagged market equity is zero, the division yields an undefined or infinite value; such outcomes are not explicitly handled beyond the missing-value drop rule. If multiple income records exist for the same identifier-month, only the first record is used, which can affect reproducibility if upstream ordering changes.

Negative computed ratios are explicitly excluded by setting them to missing before dropping missing values. The factor is timestamped at month $t$ using the month associated with the joined income and market equity records, with the market equity taken from exactly six calendar months earlier.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel containing exactly three fields: an identifier, a year-month integer in the form $YYYYMM$, and the earnings-to-price ratio value. Each row corresponds to one identifier-month where the ratio is non-missing and non-negative after applying the six-month market equity lag. The signal is intended to be interpreted as available at the month indicated by the year-month field.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix:
Income before extraordinary items is an annual accounting flow measure representing net income available to all security holders before extraordinary items and discontinued operations. Market equity is a monthly firm-level capitalization measure aggregated across share classes at the firm level, enabling consistent scaling when multiple share classes exist.

The six-month lag is implemented using calendar month subtraction rather than a fixed number of rows, so missing months break the lag link. The final year-month field is derived directly from the month timestamp as $100 \times \text{year} + \text{month}$.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: The factor measures year-over-year growth in a firm’s inventory, expressed in real terms by deflating inventory with a macro price deflator. It is designed as a monthly predictor signal aligned to each firm-month’s availability date.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction uses a firm-month panel containing firm identifier, monthly availability date, inventory, industry code, property-plant-equipment, and total assets. It also uses a monthly macro deflator series keyed by the same availability date. The output is a monthly file containing firm identifier, a $yyyymm$ month stamp, and the computed inventory growth signal.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the firm-month panel and keep only the required fields: firm identifier, availability month, inventory, industry code, property-plant-equipment, and total assets. Join the macro deflator on the availability month using an inner join so only months present in both sources remain.

Convert nominal inventory to real inventory by dividing inventory by the deflator for the same month. This produces a deflated inventory series used for all subsequent calculations.

Exclude firms whose industry code begins with 4 or 6, based on the industry code converted to a string prefix. Then require total assets to be strictly positive, and require property-plant-equipment to be positive when it is present.

Remove duplicate firm-month observations by keeping the first occurrence for each firm and availability month. Sort the remaining data by firm identifier and availability month to prepare for lag alignment.

For each firm-month, compute a calendar lag target date equal to the availability month minus 12 months. Create a lookup table mapping each firm and month to that month’s deflated inventory, then rename the month field to the lag target date and the inventory field to the 12-month lag inventory.

Merge the lookup table back to the main data on firm identifier and lag target date to retrieve the deflated inventory from exactly 12 calendar months earlier. Drop the temporary lag target date field after the merge.

Compute inventory growth as the percentage change from the 12-month lagged deflated inventory. Keep only observations where the growth value is present, then convert the availability month to an integer $yyyymm$ stamp and output the final columns.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $Inv_t$ be deflated inventory for a firm at month $t$, and let $D_t$ be the deflator at month $t$. Deflated inventory is:
$$
Inv_t = \frac{invt_t}{D_t}
$$

Let $Inv_{t-12}$ be the deflated inventory observed at the same firm’s month exactly 12 months earlier. Inventory growth is:
$$
InvGrowth_t = \frac{Inv_t}{Inv_{t-12}} - 1
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a firm-month has no matching deflator month, it is removed due to the inner join. If the firm has no observation exactly 12 calendar months earlier, the lagged inventory is missing and the growth value is dropped.

If lagged deflated inventory equals zero, the growth computation yields an infinite or undefined value depending on the environment; the procedure does not explicitly filter these cases. Duplicate firm-month records are resolved by keeping the first record encountered before lag construction.

The signal is timestamped to the firm-month availability date and then reported as $yyyymm$ derived from that availability month. The lag is calendar-based, not “12 prior rows,” so missing months break the lag link.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly predictor signal named InvGrowth. Each row corresponds to one firm and one $yyyymm$ month, with a single numeric InvGrowth value computed as the 12-month real inventory growth. Rows with missing InvGrowth are excluded from the output.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The construction follows a real (deflated) inventory growth concept, using a macro deflator to remove price-level effects before computing year-over-year change. The industry and balance-sheet filters remove specific industry prefixes and require basic balance-sheet validity consistent with the provided implementation.

factor_logic_in_paper.factor_name: Employment growth scaled by average employment
factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a firm’s employment growth over the past 12 months, scaled by the average of current and lagged employment. It is intended to capture hiring intensity in a way that is comparable across firms of different sizes.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a monthly panel containing firm identifiers, a month-end availability date, and the firm’s employee count. The employee count is the number of employees as reported, with known comparability caveats across firms and time.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the monthly panel of employee counts and remove duplicate firm–month observations, keeping the first occurrence. Then sort observations by firm and month to support time-based lag alignment.

Create a 12-month lag month for each observation by subtracting 12 calendar months from the availability month. Build a separate lag table that maps each firm and lag month to the employee count observed 12 months earlier.

Merge the lagged employee count back onto the current observation using firm and the computed lag month. This produces current employment and 12-month-lag employment on the same row when the lag exists.

Compute the hiring rate as the change in employment divided by the average of current and lagged employment. If either current or lagged employment is missing, set the hiring rate to zero.

Invalidate the signal for observations whose availability year is earlier than 1965 by setting the value to missing. After that, drop observations with missing signal values.

Convert the availability month into an integer year-month key of the form YYYYMM. Output only the firm identifier, the YYYYMM key, and the hiring rate.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $E_t$ be the employee count at month $t$, and $E_{t-12}$ be the employee count at the month exactly 12 calendar months earlier.

The hiring rate is
$$
\text{hire}_t = \frac{E_t - E_{t-12}}{0.5\,(E_t + E_{t-12})}.
$$

If $E_t$ is missing or $E_{t-12}$ is missing, then
$$
\text{hire}_t = 0.
$$

If the calendar year of $t$ is less than 1965, then $\text{hire}_t$ is set to missing and removed from the final output.
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
The 12-month lag is defined by subtracting 12 calendar months from the availability month, not by counting rows. If the exact lag month is absent for a firm, the lagged employment is missing and the signal is forced to zero.

Duplicate firm–month records are resolved by keeping the first encountered record, which can affect the lag match and the computed growth. The scaling denominator can be zero when $E_t + E_{t-12} = 0$; in that case the formula is undefined, and the implementation does not add an explicit safeguard.

The signal is aligned to the month of the availability date and then labeled by YYYYMM derived from that same month. All observations with availability years before 1965 are excluded from the final dataset.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly firm-level file containing exactly three fields: a firm identifier, an integer YYYYMM month key, and the employment-growth signal value. Each row corresponds to one firm-month, with duplicates removed as described, and with all remaining signal values non-missing.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The employee count input is an annual operating statistic that may be stale, rounded, or inconsistently defined across firms, which can introduce noise into measured growth. The factor is constructed as a monthly series by carrying the available employee count into the monthly panel and applying a 12-month calendar lag match.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a firm’s net cash distribution to shareholders, net of equity issuance, scaled by the firm’s market value of equity from six calendar months earlier. It is intended to capture payout policy in a way that combines dividends and repurchases while subtracting new share issuance.

Build a lookup table that maps each firm and month to that month’s market value of equity, then merge it back using the lag date as the key. This produces the market value of equity from exactly six calendar months earlier when available.

Compute net payout yield as dividends plus repurchase-related treasury stock amount minus stock issuance proceeds, all divided by the six-month lagged market value of equity. If the computed value equals exactly zero but at least one payout component is nonzero, replace the value with a very small positive constant to mimic floating-point behavior alignment. After that adjustment, drop observations whose net payout yield is exactly zero.

Convert the industry code to numeric and exclude firms in the financial industry range from 6000 to 6999. Also require positive book common equity, but allow missing book common equity to pass this filter.

Within each firm, order observations by month and compute a running observation count starting at one. Keep only firm-months where this count is at least 24, ensuring a minimum history length. Finally, drop missing or non-finite net payout yield values, convert the month to an integer year-month format, and output the firm identifier, year-month, and the factor value.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $t$ denote the current month and let $t-6$ denote the month exactly six calendar months earlier.

Net payouts are defined as:
$$
\text{NetPayouts}_{t} = \text{Dividends}_{t} + \text{TreasuryStockCommon}_{t} - \text{StockIssuanceProceeds}_{t}.
$$

Net payout yield is:
$$
\text{NetPayoutYield}_{t} = \frac{\text{NetPayouts}_{t}}{\text{MarketEquity}_{t-6}}.
$$

The tiny-residual adjustment is applied when $\text{NetPayoutYield}_{t} = 0$ but at least one of the three components is nonzero, setting:
$$
\text{NetPayoutYield}_{t} \leftarrow 10^{-19}.
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
The six-month lag is calendar-based, so it requires an exact match to the month that is six months earlier; if that lagged market equity is missing, the factor becomes missing and is later removed. Duplicate firm-month records are resolved by keeping the first record encountered.

Observations with an exactly zero computed factor are removed, but cases that numerically collapse to zero despite nonzero components are retained via the $10^{-19}$ substitution. Financial firms are excluded using the numeric industry code range 6000–6999, and firms with nonpositive book common equity are excluded while missing book common equity is allowed.

The minimum-history screen keeps only observations at or after the 24th available firm-month in the merged and filtered panel. The output month is represented as an integer $100 \times \text{year} + \text{month}$ derived from the monthly timestamp.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly firm-level file containing exactly three fields: firm identifier as an integer, year-month as an integer in YYYYMM format, and net payout yield as a numeric value. Each row corresponds to a unique firm-month after all filters, with net payout yield guaranteed to be non-missing and finite, and not exactly zero.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Dividends are total cash dividends on common stock for the period. The repurchase-related component uses the treasury stock amount for common shares as provided, and issuance is measured by net proceeds from selling stock. Book common equity is used only as a screening variable, not in the factor numerator or denominator.

factor_logic_in_paper.factor_name: Net debt financing scaled by average total assets
factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a firm’s net debt financing activity over the period, scaled by average total assets, to make financing intensity comparable across firms of different sizes. It captures net cash inflows from issuing and retiring long-term debt, plus the change in current debt, normalized by an average asset base.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses the change in debt in current liabilities, long-term debt issued, long-term debt retired, and total assets. It also uses an identifier for the security and a monthly availability timestamp to align observations and construct a 12-month lag of total assets.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, ensure there is at most one observation per security and monthly availability timestamp. If duplicates exist, keep the first occurrence and discard the rest.

Next, sort observations by security and monthly availability timestamp. Replace missing values of the change in current debt with zero.

Then, create a 12-month lag of total assets within each security. This lag is used to form an average total assets denominator.

Compute net debt financing as long-term debt issued minus long-term debt retired plus the change in current debt. Scale this net flow by average total assets, defined as one-half of current total assets plus the 12-month lagged total assets.

Finally, apply an outlier screen by setting the factor value to missing when its absolute value exceeds 1. Keep only non-missing factor values for output, and convert the monthly availability timestamp into an integer year-month key.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let net debt financing flow be
$$
\text{NetDebtFlow}_t = \text{LongTermDebtIssued}_t - \text{LongTermDebtRetired}_t + \text{ChangeInCurrentDebt}_t.
$$

Let average total assets be
$$
\text{AvgAssets}_t = 0.5 \times \left(\text{TotalAssets}_t + \text{TotalAssets}_{t-12}\right).
$$

The factor is
$$
\text{NetDebtFinance}_t = \frac{\text{NetDebtFlow}_t}{\text{AvgAssets}_t}.
$$

Apply the outlier rule
$$
\text{NetDebtFinance}_t = \text{missing} \quad \text{if} \quad \left|\text{NetDebtFinance}_t\right| > 1.
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If the change in current debt is missing, it is treated as zero, which assumes no reported change rather than unknown activity. If the 12-month lag of total assets is missing, the denominator cannot be formed and the factor becomes missing.

If average total assets equals zero, the ratio is undefined; the implementation will yield a missing or non-finite value that should not be output. Duplicate security–month records are resolved by keeping the first record, which can affect a small number of observations.

The factor is timestamped to the monthly availability date used in the input and then mapped to an integer year-month key. The output includes only months where the factor is non-missing after the outlier screen.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel keyed by security identifier and integer year-month. The delivered value is the net debt financing factor as a floating-point number, with extreme values removed by the absolute-value threshold.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix:
Change in current debt represents the net increase or decrease in short-term debt and the current portion of long-term debt from a cash-flow perspective. Long-term debt issued and retired represent gross proceeds and repayments, respectively, and may be reported with firm-specific netting conventions.

Total assets is used to scale financing activity by firm size, and the denominator uses the average of current and 12-month lagged assets. The outlier filter at $|\text{NetDebtFinance}|>1$ is a hard exclusion rule that removes unusually large scaled financing values.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures past trading activity in dollar terms using a two-month lag. It is intended as a dollar volume predictor in the spirit of Brennan, Chordia, and Subrahmanyam (1998), using lagged volume and lagged price.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a monthly panel containing a security identifier, a month-end availability timestamp, monthly trading volume measured in shares, and the month-end price in USD per share. The price field is treated in absolute value to neutralize signed storage conventions.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, order each security’s monthly observations by the month-end availability timestamp. Then create a two-month lag of monthly trading volume and a two-month lag of month-end price within each security.

Next, compute lagged dollar volume as the product of the two-month lagged volume and the absolute value of the two-month lagged price. Apply a natural logarithm to this product to form the signal.

Then remove observations where the signal is missing, which typically occurs when the two-month lag is unavailable. Keep only the security identifier, the month-end availability timestamp, and the computed signal.

Next, convert the month-end availability timestamp into an integer year-month key of the form $YYYYMM$. Cast both the security identifier and the year-month key to 64-bit integers for consistency.

Finally, retain only the security identifier, the year-month key, and the signal, and set the index to the pair of security identifier and year-month key. The resulting dataset is written as a monthly predictor file.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $t$ denote the current month for a given security, and let $\mathrm{VOL}_t$ be monthly trading volume in shares and $\mathrm{PRC}_t$ be the month-end price in USD per share.

Define the two-month lags as:
$$
\mathrm{VOL}_{t-2} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{PRC}_{t-2}.
$$

Define the dollar volume predictor as:
$$
\mathrm{DolVol}_t = \ln\!\Big(\mathrm{VOL}_{t-2} \cdot \lvert \mathrm{PRC}_{t-2} \rvert\Big).
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
The first two months of each security’s history have undefined two-month lags, so the signal is missing and must be dropped. If either lagged volume or lagged price is missing, the signal is missing and is dropped.

If the lagged price is negative due to signed storage conventions, its absolute value is used before multiplication. If the lagged dollar volume product is non-positive, the logarithm is undefined; such cases will result in missing or invalid values and should not appear in the final output after dropping missing signals.

The signal dated $t$ uses information from $t-2$ only, so it is a two-month-lagged predictor aligned to the month identified by the year-month key derived from the availability timestamp.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel indexed by security identifier and integer year-month key $YYYYMM$. It contains a single column named DolVol holding the natural log of two-month lagged dollar volume as defined above, with rows containing missing signals removed.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Trading volume is monthly trading volume measured in shares. Price is the month-end price in USD per share and is taken in absolute value to address signed price conventions. DolVol is a constructed monthly predictor representing the log of two-month lagged dollar trading volume.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a firm’s research and development spending scaled by its market value of equity. It is intended to capture R&D intensity in the spirit of Chan, Lakonishok, and Sougiannis (2001).
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a monthly firm identifier, a monthly availability timestamp, a firm-level market equity measure aggregated across share classes, and a monthly R&D expenditure item. The market equity input is a firm-level market capitalization aggregated at the firm level across all linked share classes for that month, expressed in currency units consistent with the R&D item’s currency scaling. The R&D expenditure input is the firm’s reported R&D spending aligned to the same monthly availability timestamp used for merging.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the monthly firm mapping and market equity data, and remove rows where the accounting identifier is missing. This ensures the accounting merge key is present.

Merge the remaining rows with the monthly accounting dataset on the accounting identifier and the monthly availability timestamp. Use an inner join so only months with both market equity and R&D expenditure are retained.

Compute the signal as R&D expenditure divided by firm-level market equity. Store the result as the factor value.

Remove observations where the computed factor value is missing. Then convert the monthly availability timestamp into an integer year-month key of the form $YYYYMM$.

Keep only the firm identifier, the $YYYYMM$ key, and the factor value. Output the resulting panel as a monthly signal file.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
For each firm-month observation, define R&D intensity as
$$
RD_{t} = \frac{XRD_{t}}{MVE_{t}}
$$
where $XRD_{t}$ is monthly R&D expenditure and $MVE_{t}$ is firm-level market equity aggregated across share classes in the same month.

The year-month key is constructed from the availability timestamp as
$$
yyyymm = 100 \times year(time) + month(time)
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If the accounting identifier is missing for a firm-month, that observation is excluded before merging. If either R&D expenditure or market equity is unavailable at the merged firm-month, the inner join drops the observation.

If market equity is zero, the division yields an undefined or infinite value; such cases are not explicitly filtered beyond the missing-value drop, so downstream handling should treat non-finite values as invalid if they occur. The signal is timestamped to the monthly availability date used in both sources, and the output month key is derived directly from that timestamp.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel with one row per firm identifier and month, containing the computed R&D intensity value. The file contains exactly three columns: a firm identifier, an integer $YYYYMM$ month key, and the factor value labeled as R&D over market equity. Observations with missing factor values are excluded from the output.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Market equity is the firm-level capitalization aggregated across all share classes linked to the same firm in that month, which supports consistent scaling across multi-class firms. The factor is a simple ratio and does not apply winsorization, industry adjustment, or lagging beyond the availability timestamp alignment used in the merge.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures the time-series volatility of a stock’s share turnover, defined as trading volume scaled by shares outstanding. It follows the construction in Chordia, Subrahmanyam, and Anshuman (2001), using a 36-month rolling window and then restricting the signal to smaller-size stocks.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction uses monthly trading volume, monthly shares outstanding, and month-end price. It also uses a monthly availability timestamp to align observations and to form same-month size quintiles. The final output is the monthly share turnover volatility signal.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Compute monthly share turnover as trading volume divided by shares outstanding. Compute market equity as shares outstanding times the absolute value of month-end price.

Within each stock, sort observations by the monthly timestamp. Compute the rolling standard deviation of monthly turnover using a 36-month window.

Require at least 24 non-missing monthly turnover observations inside the rolling window. If fewer than 24 observations are available, the rolling standard deviation is missing.

For each month, sort stocks by market equity and assign size quintiles using five equal-frequency bins. If ties or insufficient unique values prevent five bins, use the maximum feasible number of bins.

Set the signal to missing for stocks in the two largest size quintiles for that month. Keep the computed value only for stocks in the three smallest size quintiles.

Return the stock identifier, the monthly timestamp, and the final signal value. The signal is aligned to the same month as the inputs used in its computation.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Monthly turnover:
$$
\text{turnover}_{i,t} = \frac{\text{volume}_{i,t}}{\text{shares\_outstanding}_{i,t}}
$$

Market equity used for size ranking:
$$
\text{market\_equity}_{i,t} = \text{shares\_outstanding}_{i,t}\cdot \left|\text{price}_{i,t}\right|
$$

Rolling turnover volatility (within stock $i$), with window length 36 months and minimum 24 observations:
$$
\text{std\_turn}_{i,t} = \operatorname{StdDev}\left(\text{turnover}_{i,t-35},\ldots,\text{turnover}_{i,t}\right)
$$
computed only if at least 24 values in the window are non-missing.

Size filter applied each month $t$:
$$
\text{std\_turn}_{i,t} \leftarrow \text{missing} \quad \text{if size\_quintile}_{i,t}\in\{4,5\}
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If shares outstanding is zero or missing, turnover is undefined and should be treated as missing, which can propagate to the rolling statistic. If price is negative in the raw source, use its absolute value when computing market equity.

If a month has too few distinct market equity values to form five equal-frequency bins, the size binning may produce fewer than five groups. In that case, only stocks assigned to groups labeled 4 or higher are nulled, and others retain the signal.

The rolling standard deviation is computed using information up to and including month $t$. The output is timestamped at month $t$ and is not lagged further by this specification.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel keyed by stock identifier and monthly timestamp. The value is a floating signal representing the 36-month rolling standard deviation of monthly turnover, subject to the size-based missingness rule. Missing values occur when the rolling window has fewer than 24 observations or when the stock is in the top two size quintiles that month.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Trading volume is measured in shares traded over the month, and shares outstanding are typically recorded in thousands of shares; the turnover ratio follows the direct division as provided by the inputs. The size restriction intentionally removes the largest stocks by setting their signal to missing, matching the described “tiny spread” implementation choice.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a firm’s annual growth rate in total assets, expressed as a percentage change relative to total assets from twelve months earlier. It is intended to capture balance-sheet expansion over a one-year horizon using monthly-aligned accounting availability dates.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses firm identifiers, a monthly time index representing when accounting data are available, and total assets. Total assets are the balance-sheet total, reported in currency units (commonly millions of USD), and may be affected by restatements and acquisition accounting.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, align observations into a firm-by-time panel using the firm identifier and the monthly availability timestamp. Then sort within each firm by the monthly availability timestamp to ensure lags reference the correct prior observations.

Next, create a twelve-month lag of total assets by shifting the total-assets series back by twelve monthly observations within each firm. This lag represents the total assets available exactly one year earlier in the same monthly panel.

Then compute asset growth as the percentage change from the twelve-month lagged total assets to the current total assets. If the lagged total assets equals zero, set the factor value to missing to avoid division by zero.

Finally, retain the computed asset growth as the published predictor value at each firm-month where inputs are available. Missing inputs naturally propagate to missing outputs through the lag and arithmetic.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $A_t$ be total assets at month $t$ in the monthly availability panel, and let $A_{t-12}$ be the value from twelve months earlier.

The factor is
$$
\text{AssetGrowth}_t = \frac{A_t - A_{t-12}}{A_{t-12}}.
$$

If $A_{t-12} = 0$, then $\text{AssetGrowth}_t$ is missing.
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
For the first twelve monthly observations of each firm, the twelve-month lag is unavailable, so the factor is missing. If the lagged total assets is zero, the factor is set to missing rather than infinite or undefined.

If current total assets is missing, or if the lagged value is missing due to gaps in the monthly panel, the factor is missing. The factor is timestamped at the monthly availability date used for the current total assets, and it uses only information available as of that timestamp.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly firm-level predictor equal to the computed asset growth value. The output is missing when the twelve-month lag is unavailable, when the lagged total assets is zero, or when required inputs are missing.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Total assets are defined as the sum of current and noncurrent assets as reported on the balance sheet, and historical values may change due to restatements. Asset growth is a constructed signal derived mechanically from total assets and its twelve-month lag in the monthly availability panel.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures net equity issuance over a five-year horizon, adjusted for the stock’s own buy-and-hold performance. It is designed to capture changes in market value that are not explained by price appreciation alone, consistent with the composite issuance concept in Daniel and Titman (2006).
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction uses a monthly total stock return series and a monthly market equity series. The return is a decimal monthly total return aligned to the month of availability. The market equity is the stock’s monthly market capitalization at the share-class level.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, order observations within each stock by the monthly availability timestamp to ensure lags and cumulative products follow calendar time. Then build a cumulative return index that starts at 1 and compounds by multiplying $(1+\text{return})$ each month.

Next, create 60-month lags of the cumulative return index and of market equity. The lag must be calendar-valid, meaning it refers to the observation exactly 60 months earlier for the same stock.

Then compute the 60-month buy-and-hold return using the cumulative return index and its 60-month lag. This produces the stock’s compounded return over the prior five years.

Finally, compute composite equity issuance as the log growth in market equity over 60 months minus the 60-month buy-and-hold return. The result is recorded as the monthly signal for that stock-month.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $r_{i,t}$ be the monthly total return for stock $i$ at month $t$. Define the cumulative return index
$$
I_{i,t}=\prod_{\tau \le t}(1+r_{i,\tau}),
$$
with initialization at 1 at the first available month for each stock.

Define the 60-month buy-and-hold return
$$
BH_{i,t}=\frac{I_{i,t}-I_{i,t-60}}{I_{i,t-60}}.
$$

Let $ME_{i,t}$ be market equity. Composite equity issuance is
$$
CEI_{i,t}=\ln\!\left(\frac{ME_{i,t}}{ME_{i,t-60}}\right)-BH_{i,t}.
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a stock lacks a calendar-valid observation 60 months earlier, the signal is missing for that month. If the lagged cumulative index is missing, the buy-and-hold return and the signal are missing.

If $ME_{i,t}$ or $ME_{i,t-60}$ is missing, the signal is missing. If $ME_{i,t-60}\le 0$ or $ME_{i,t}\le 0$, the log ratio is undefined and the signal should be treated as missing.

The signal is computed at the monthly availability timestamp and uses information through that same month, plus the calendar-valid value from 60 months earlier. No additional publication lag is introduced beyond the provided monthly availability alignment.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly stock-level predictor named Composite equity issuance. It is defined for stock-months with non-missing monthly returns and market equity sufficient to form calendar-valid 60-month lags. The value is a real number with no explicit winsorization, standardization, or cross-sectional demeaning applied in this construction.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix:
Interpretation: positive values indicate market equity grew more than can be explained by the stock’s own five-year buy-and-hold return, consistent with net equity issuance. Negative values indicate market equity growth lagged what would be implied by price performance, consistent with net repurchases or shrinking equity base.

Implementation note: the buy-and-hold return is computed from a cumulative product index rather than summing returns, ensuring compounding over the full 60-month window.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures long-horizon past performance to capture long-run reversal effects documented in the academic literature. It summarizes a stock’s compounded return from 36 months ago through 13 months ago, ending one year before the current month.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a monthly stock return series and a monthly availability date for each stock-month observation. The return is a decimal monthly total return, and the availability date is used to align the signal to a year-month timestamp.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the monthly stock return series and sort observations by stock identifier and monthly availability date. Replace missing monthly returns with zero before any lagging or compounding.

For each stock and month $t$, create lagged monthly returns for lags 13 through 36 months. Each lag represents the return observed at $t-k$ for $k \in \{13,\dots,36\}$.

Compute the compounded return across the 24 lagged months by multiplying $(1+\text{return})$ across all lags. Subtract 1 from the product to convert the gross compounded return into a net compounded return.

Drop stock-month rows where the long-run reversal value is missing due to insufficient history. Convert the monthly availability date into an integer year-month key and keep only the stock identifier, year-month key, and the signal.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $r_{t-k}$ be the monthly return $k$ months before month $t$, after replacing missing monthly returns with $0$.

The long-run reversal signal at month $t$ is
$$
\text{LRreversal}_t = \prod_{k=13}^{36} (1 + r_{t-k}) - 1.
$$

The year-month key is
$$
\text{yyyymm} = 100 \cdot \text{year}(\text{date}) + \text{month}(\text{date}).
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a stock lacks any of the required lagged months from $t-36$ through $t-13$, the compounded product is undefined and the signal is treated as missing for that month. Those missing-signal rows are removed from the final output.

Because missing monthly returns are replaced with $0$ before lagging, a missing return within the lookback window contributes a factor of $(1+0)=1$ to the product. This choice prevents missing returns from mechanically forcing the compounded return to be missing.

The signal is timestamped to the month of the availability date used in the input table. The lookback window ends at $t-13$, leaving a 12-month gap between the end of the return window and the signal month.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract:
The output is a monthly panel keyed by stock identifier and integer year-month. For each key, it provides a single numeric value named LRreversal equal to the compounded net return from months $t-36$ to $t-13$.

The output contains only rows where LRreversal is non-missing. The stock identifier and year-month key are stored as integers for consistency.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The construction uses 24 monthly lags, corresponding exactly to months $t-36$ through $t-13$ inclusive. The compounding is multiplicative, not a sum of returns, so it reflects total growth over the window.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor estimates the duration of equity by treating equity value as the present value of projected future cash distributions to equity holders and measuring the weighted-average timing of those distributions. The construction follows a fixed-horizon projection with mean-reverting profitability and growth, then maps the annual estimate to a monthly panel.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses annual common equity, income before extraordinary items, and sales to form profitability, growth, and implied cash distributions to equity. It also uses fiscal-year-end price and shares outstanding to compute market equity for scaling. Timing fields identifying the fiscal year and the associated statement date are used for ordering and for selecting the most recent available record when multiple statements map to the same month.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Sort each firm’s annual records in fiscal-year order to create one-year lags. Compute a contemporaneous return on equity as income divided by lagged common equity. Compute an equity growth proxy as the percentage change in sales from the prior year, treating undefined growth from zero prior sales as missing.

Use lagged common equity, the return on equity, and the growth proxy to infer a current-period cash distribution to equity. When the growth proxy is missing, treat it as zero only for the cash-distribution calculation. This yields a baseline cash distribution series aligned with the annual record.

Project return on equity forward with partial mean reversion toward a constant cost of equity. Project the growth proxy forward with partial mean reversion toward a constant long-run growth rate. Use the projected growth to roll book equity forward, and use projected profitability and book equity dynamics to generate projected cash distributions for years 1 through 10.

Discount each projected cash distribution at a constant cost of equity to compute two present-value aggregates. The first aggregate is the present value of cash distributions. The second aggregate is the present value of time-weighted cash distributions, where each year’s cash distribution is multiplied by its horizon.

Compute market equity as fiscal-year-end price times shares outstanding. Combine the discounted aggregates and market equity to form the equity duration measure, including a terminal-value adjustment beyond year 10. The terminal adjustment uses a closed-form duration term consistent with a perpetuity discounted at the same cost of equity.

Expand each annual observation into 12 monthly observations starting from the availability month. Assign the same annual equity duration value to each of the 12 months, shifting the month forward by 0 through 11 months. This creates a monthly panel with a stepwise-constant signal between annual updates.

When multiple firm records map to the same firm-month, keep the record with the latest statement date. When multiple identifiers map to the same security-month, keep a single record after sorting to prefer non-missing equity duration, then the latest statement date. Drop observations with missing equity duration before final output.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $t$ index fiscal years for a given firm, and let lagged values refer to the prior fiscal year.

Return on equity:
$$
ROE_t = \frac{IB_t}{CEQ_{t-1}}
$$

Sales-based growth proxy:
$$
g_t = \frac{SALE_t}{SALE_{t-1}} - 1
$$
If $SALE_{t-1}=0$, then $g_t$ is treated as missing.

Implied cash distribution to equity for the current year, using $g_t$ filled with zero only in this expression:
$$
CD_t = CEQ_{t-1}\left(ROE_t - \tilde{g}_t\right)
$$
where $\tilde{g}_t = g_t$ if observed, else $0$.

Constants used in projections:
$$
\rho_{roe}=0.57,\quad r=0.12,\quad \rho_g=0.24,\quad g^{LR}=0.06
$$

One-step-ahead projected return on equity and growth:
$$
ROE_{t,1} = \rho_{roe}\,ROE_t + (1-\rho_{roe})\,r
$$
$$
g_{t,1} = \rho_g\,\tilde{g}_t + (1-\rho_g)\,g^{LR}
$$

Projected book equity and cash distribution for horizon 1:
$$
BV_{t,1} = CEQ_t(1+g_{t,1})
$$
$$
CD_{t,1} = CEQ_t - BV_{t,1} + CEQ_t\,ROE_{t,1}
$$

For horizons $k=2,\dots,10$, with $j=k-1$:
$$
ROE_{t,k} = \rho_{roe}\,ROE_{t,j} + (1-\rho_{roe})\,r
$$
$$
g_{t,k} = \rho_g\,\tilde{g}_{t,j} + (1-\rho_g)\,g^{LR}
$$
$$
BV_{t,k} = BV_{t,j}(1+g_{t,k})
$$
$$
CD_{t,k} = BV_{t,j} - BV_{t,k} + BV_{t,j}\,ROE_{t,k}
$$
where $\tilde{g}_{t,j}$ is the prior projected growth with missing treated as zero in the recursion.

Discount factor:
$$
D = 1+r
$$

Present-value aggregates over horizons 1 to 10:
$$
PV = \sum_{k=1}^{10}\frac{CD_{t,k}}{D^k}
$$
$$
MD = \sum_{k=1}^{10}\frac{k\cdot CD_{t,k}}{D^k}
$$

Market equity:
$$
ME_t = PRCC\_F_t \cdot CSHO_t
$$

Equity duration:
$$
EquityDuration_t = \frac{MD}{ME_t} + \left(10+\frac{1+r}{r}\right)\left(1-\frac{PV}{ME_t}\right)
$$

Monthly mapping: for each annual record available in month $m$, assign the same $EquityDuration_t$ to months $m, m+1, \dots, m+11$.
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If lagged common equity is missing or zero, return on equity is undefined and will propagate to missing projections and a missing final signal. If prior-year sales are zero, the growth proxy is set to missing; it is replaced by zero only where explicitly required for cash-distribution and growth-projection steps.

If market equity is missing or zero, scaling terms $MD/ME_t$ and $PV/ME_t$ are undefined, producing a missing signal that is removed from the final output. Infinite growth values from division by zero are treated as missing before any filling rules are applied.

The annual signal is assumed available starting at the provided availability month and is carried forward for the next 12 months. When multiple annual statements map into the same month, the most recent statement date is used, and ties across identifiers are resolved by preferring non-missing signals.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly predictor indexed by security identifier and calendar year-month. Each record contains a single numeric value representing equity duration for that security-month. Observations with missing values are excluded from the delivered file.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The method uses fixed parameters for mean reversion in profitability and growth, a constant cost of equity for discounting, and a 10-year explicit forecast horizon with a terminal adjustment. The monthly panel is created by mechanically expanding each annual observation into 12 consecutive months starting from the availability month, then deduplicating by recency and non-missingness.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures operating cash flow scaled by the market value of equity. It follows the operating cash flows to price construction referenced in Desai, Rajgopal, and Venkatachalam (2004), using a monthly availability timestamp.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation requires a monthly panel keyed by a security identifier and a monthly availability date, containing current assets, cash and short-term investments, current liabilities, debt in current liabilities, income taxes payable, depreciation expense, income before extraordinary items, and operating cash flow from the cash flow statement. It also requires the market value of equity at the same monthly availability date.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from a monthly dataset that contains both accounting items and the market value of equity for the same security and availability month. If multiple records exist for the same security and month, keep only the first.

For each security and month, construct 12-month lags of the balance-sheet items used in accruals. The lag must be calendar-based, meaning the lagged value is taken from exactly 12 months earlier, not from the prior row.

Compute an accrual component using changes in non-cash current assets and changes in current liabilities net of short-term debt and taxes payable, and then adjust by depreciation. This accrual component is used to convert earnings into an operating cash flow proxy when a direct cash flow measure is unavailable.

Compute a preliminary operating cash flow measure as income before extraordinary items minus the accrual component. Scale this preliminary cash flow by the market value of equity to obtain the initial ratio, and set the ratio to missing when the market value of equity equals zero.

If operating cash flow from the cash flow statement is available for that security and month, replace the initial ratio with operating cash flow divided by the market value of equity. Apply the same division-by-zero rule when the market value of equity equals zero.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $t$ denote the monthly availability date and let $t-12$ denote the date exactly 12 months earlier.

Define the 12-month changes as $\Delta X_t = X_t - X_{t-12}$ for each lagged balance-sheet item.

Accrual component:
$$
\text{accrual}_t
=
\left(\Delta \text{current assets}_t - \Delta \text{cash}_t\right)
-
\left(\Delta \text{current liabilities}_t - \Delta \text{short-term debt}_t - \Delta \text{taxes payable}_t - \text{depreciation}_t\right)
$$

Calculated operating cash flow proxy:
$$
\widehat{\text{operating cash flow}}_t
=
\text{income before extraordinary items}_t - \text{accrual}_t
$$

Initial operating cash flow to price ratio:
$$
\text{ratio}_t
=
\begin{cases}
\frac{\widehat{\text{operating cash flow}}_t}{\text{market value of equity}_t}, & \text{if } \text{market value of equity}_t \neq 0 \\
\text{missing}, & \text{if } \text{market value of equity}_t = 0
\end{cases}
$$

Override when reported operating cash flow is available:
$$
\text{ratio}_t
\leftarrow
\begin{cases}
\frac{\text{reported operating cash flow}_t}{\text{market value of equity}_t}, & \text{if reported operating cash flow}_t \text{ is available and } \text{market value of equity}_t \neq 0 \\
\text{missing}, & \text{if reported operating cash flow}_t \text{ is available and } \text{market value of equity}_t = 0
\end{cases}
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If the 12-month lag for any required balance-sheet item is missing, the accrual component becomes missing and the calculated cash flow proxy becomes missing. In that case, the ratio is still produced if reported operating cash flow is available and the market value of equity is nonzero.

If the market value of equity is zero, the ratio is set to missing regardless of whether the numerator is available. Missing numerators propagate to a missing ratio unless the reported operating cash flow override applies.

The lag is defined by calendar month alignment, so gaps in the monthly panel do not imply using the previous observation as a lag. The factor is timestamped at the monthly availability date used to align accounting data and market value of equity.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly numeric signal equal to operating cash flow divided by market value of equity, keyed by security identifier and monthly availability date. The value is missing when the market value of equity is zero, and otherwise reflects reported operating cash flow when available, falling back to the accrual-based proxy.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The accrual-based proxy implements an indirect-method mapping from earnings to operating cash flow by removing working-capital accruals and adding back depreciation. The replacement with reported operating cash flow ensures the factor uses the cash flow statement measure when it exists, while maintaining coverage when it does not.
