factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures financial distress risk using an O-Score bankruptcy predictor and converts it into a monthly binary signal based on cross-sectional decile ranks. The intent is to identify the highest-distress firms each month and flag them with a value of 1, while assigning 0 to a broader set of lower-distress firms.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction requires firm identifiers, a monthly availability timestamp, and accounting items for assets, liabilities, working capital components, profitability, and operating cash flow. It also requires a monthly price field for alignment and a monthly deflator series to scale assets in real terms. An industry classification code is used to exclude certain industries from signal formation.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the monthly firm-accounting panel and keep only the required identifier, timestamp, accounting fields, and industry code. Remove duplicate firm-month observations, then inner-join the monthly price field and the monthly deflator on the same firm-month and month keys.

Replace missing funds-from-operations with operating cash flow for the same firm-month. Create a 12-month lag of income before extraordinary items using a calendar month offset, and merge that lagged value back by firm and lagged month.

Compute the O-Score using the specified linear combination of transformed ratios and indicator terms. Use safe division so any zero or missing denominator yields a missing ratio, and use a safe logarithm so nonpositive or missing inputs yield a missing log term.

Convert the industry code to numeric and set the O-Score to missing for excluded industries. Then, within each month, assign firms to deciles based on the O-Score using quantile cuts, allowing fewer than ten bins if ties prevent full decile formation.

Reset the continuous O-Score and replace it with a binary signal. Assign 1 to firms in the highest O-Score decile, assign 0 to firms in deciles 1 through 7, and leave other deciles missing.

Keep only firm identifier, month, and the binary signal, and drop rows where the signal is missing. Convert the month timestamp into an integer year-month key of the form $YYYYMM$, cast identifiers and the year-month key to integers, and index the output by firm and year-month.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Define safe operators used in the construction as follows:
$$
\operatorname{safe\_div}(a,b)=
\begin{cases}
\text{missing}, & b=0 \text{ or } b \text{ is missing} \\
a/b, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$
$$
\operatorname{safe\_log}(x)=
\begin{cases}
\text{missing}, & x\le 0 \text{ or } x \text{ is missing} \\
\ln(x), & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Let $A$ be total assets, $L$ total liabilities, $CA$ current assets, $CL$ current liabilities, $IB$ income before extraordinary items, $IB_{-12}$ its 12-month lag, $FOPT$ funds-from-operations (with missing values replaced by operating cash flow), and $D$ the deflator. The O-Score is:
$$
\begin{aligned}
O =\;& -1.32
-0.407\cdot \operatorname{safe\_log}\!\left(\frac{A}{D}\right)
+6.03\cdot \operatorname{safe\_div}(L,A)
-1.43\cdot \operatorname{safe\_div}(CA-CL,A) \\
&+0.076\cdot \operatorname{safe\_div}(CL,CA)
-1.72\cdot \mathbb{1}[L>A]
-2.37\cdot \operatorname{safe\_div}(IB,A)
-1.83\cdot \operatorname{safe\_div}(FOPT,L) \\
&+0.285\cdot \mathbb{1}[IB+IB_{-12}<0]
-0.521\cdot \operatorname{safe\_div}\!\left(IB-IB_{-12}, |IB|+|IB_{-12}|\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Industry exclusion is applied by setting $O$ to missing when the numeric industry code is in the interval $(3999,5000)$ or greater than $5999$. Decile ranks are computed each month from the cross-section of non-missing $O$, producing an integer decile label in $\{1,\dots,10\}$ when ten bins are feasible.

The final binary signal $S$ is:
$$
S=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{decile}(O)=10 \\
0, & \text{decile}(O)\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\} \\
\text{missing}, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

The year-month key is:
$$
YYYYMM = 100\cdot \text{year}(\text{month}) + \text{month}(\text{month}).
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a firm-month has missing or invalid inputs that trigger safe division or safe logarithm, the O-Score may become missing and the observation will not receive a signal. If the 12-month lagged income value is unavailable, lag-dependent terms may be missing and can propagate to a missing O-Score.

If the month’s cross-section has too many ties or too few valid observations, quantile binning may produce fewer than ten bins. In that case, the “top decile” label may not exist, and no firm will be assigned a value of 1 for that month.

The construction uses the month-level availability timestamp as the timing anchor for merging and ranking. The output month key is derived directly from that timestamp, so the signal is aligned to the same month in which the inputs are available.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly, firm-level binary predictor taking values in $\{0,1\}$ only, with missing values removed. The index is the pair (firm identifier, integer $YYYYMM$), and the single data field is the binary O-Score signal.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Funds-from-operations is imputed with operating cash flow when missing to increase coverage while preserving the intended cash-flow-based component. The industry exclusions remove firms in regulated or structurally different sectors as defined by the specified industry code ranges, ensuring comparability of distress signals across the remaining universe.

factor_logic_in_paper.factor_name: Growth in long-term net operating assets (GrLTNOA)
factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures annual growth in long-term net operating assets, adjusted to remove working-capital-related accrual effects. It is designed to capture longer-horizon operating asset expansion consistent with the Fairfield, Whisenant, and Yohn (2003) decomposition logic.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction requires firm identifiers and a monthly availability timestamp, plus balance-sheet components for operating assets and operating liabilities, total assets, and depreciation expense. Specifically, it uses total receivables, inventories, net property plant and equipment, other current assets, intangible assets, other noncurrent assets, accounts payable, other current liabilities, other noncurrent liabilities, total assets, and depreciation.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the monthly panel of accounting observations keyed by firm and month of data availability. Remove duplicate firm-month rows, keeping the first occurrence, then sort by firm and month.

Create 12-month lags for each balance-sheet input used in the long-term net operating assets definition and for total assets. These lags align the current observation with the same firm’s value from 12 months earlier.

Compute long-term net operating assets for the current month and for the 12-month lagged month. Scale each by total assets from the same month to form asset-scaled levels.

Compute a working-capital adjustment using 12-month changes in selected current operating assets and current operating liabilities, subtracting depreciation. Scale this adjustment by average total assets over the current and lagged months.

Define the factor as the difference between the current and lagged asset-scaled long-term net operating assets, minus the working-capital adjustment. The resulting value is recorded for each firm-month where all required components are available.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Long-term net operating assets (level) at time $t$ is
$$
LTNOA_t = REC_t + INV_t + PPENT_t + ACO_t + INTAN_t + AO_t - AP_t - LCO_t - LO_t.
$$

Asset-scaled long-term net operating assets at time $t$ and $t-12$ are
$$
CLT_t = \frac{LTNOA_t}{AT_t}, \qquad CLT_{t-12} = \frac{LTNOA_{t-12}}{AT_{t-12}}.
$$

Average total assets used for scaling the adjustment is
$$
\overline{AT}_t = \frac{AT_t + AT_{t-12}}{2}.
$$

Working-capital adjustment at time $t$ is
$$
WCA_t =
\frac{
(REC_t-REC_{t-12}) + (INV_t-INV_{t-12}) + (ACO_t-ACO_{t-12})
- \left[(AP_t-AP_{t-12}) + (LCO_t-LCO_{t-12})\right]
- DP_t
}{\overline{AT}_t}.
$$

The factor value is
$$
GrLTNOA_t = CLT_t - CLT_{t-12} - WCA_t.
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a firm-month lacks a 12-month lag for any required lagged component, the factor is undefined for that month. If total assets at $t$ or $t-12$ are missing or zero, scaling is invalid and the factor is undefined.

Depreciation is used as provided for the current period in the adjustment term; no lagged depreciation is required. The signal is timestamped to the month of data availability and uses information from that month and the observation 12 months earlier.

Duplicate firm-month records are resolved deterministically by keeping the first encountered record before sorting. This choice can affect results if duplicates differ in values.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly firm-level numeric signal named GrLTNOA. Each output row corresponds to a unique firm and month of data availability, with GrLTNOA populated only when all required inputs and lags support the computation.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Economic interpretation: higher values indicate faster growth in long-term operating assets after removing working-capital-related accrual movements, aiming to isolate longer-term operating investment changes. Construction notes: long-term net operating assets include both current operating asset components and selected noncurrent operating assets, net of operating liabilities, and the adjustment removes short-term operating accrual changes and depreciation scaled by average assets.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: The factor measures a firm’s book-to-market ratio by scaling book equity by a December market equity value that is carried forward, following the calendar-timing convention used in classic value-factor constructions.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction uses monthly firm observations that include a firm identifier, an availability month timestamp, end-of-month price, shares outstanding, deferred taxes and investment tax credit, multiple measures of shareholders’ equity, total assets, total liabilities, and multiple preferred stock fields. The output is a monthly signal representing book equity divided by an appropriately lagged December market equity.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the intersection of the accounting panel and the monthly market panel on firm identifier and availability month. Keep only one record per firm-month from the accounting side, then sort by firm and month.

Extract the calendar month and year from the availability month. Compute market equity only in December as absolute end-of-month price times shares outstanding, and leave it missing in other months.

Within each firm-year, propagate the December market equity to all months by taking the single non-missing December value for that firm-year. This produces a firm-year December market equity field that is constant across months in the same calendar year.

Set deferred taxes and investment tax credit to zero when missing. Construct preferred stock as the first available value among carrying value, redemption value, and liquidating value.

Construct shareholders’ equity using a priority rule. Use total stockholders’ equity when available, otherwise use common equity plus preferred stock, and if still missing use total assets minus total liabilities.

Compute book equity as shareholders’ equity plus deferred taxes and investment tax credit minus preferred stock. This yields a book equity measure aligned to the same firm-month record.

Create two calendar-based lag dates for each month: 12 months prior and 17 months prior. Use these lag dates to look up the December market equity value that was assigned to those prior months for the same firm.

Compute two candidate book-to-market ratios by dividing current book equity by the 12-month-lagged December market equity and by the 17-month-lagged December market equity. If the denominator equals zero, set the ratio to missing.

Select which candidate ratio to use based on the current calendar month. For months June through December, use the 12-month-lagged version; for months January through May, use the 17-month-lagged version.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
December market equity for a month $t$ is
$$
ME^{Dec}_t =
\begin{cases}
|P_t|\cdot SHROUT_t, & \text{if } month(t)=12 \\
\text{missing}, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Firm-year December market equity assigned to each month $t$ in calendar year $y$ is
$$
DecME_{i,y} = \min_{t \in \{i,y\}} ME^{Dec}_t
$$
where the minimum effectively selects the single non-missing December value within the firm-year.

Preferred stock is defined as the first non-missing among the available preferred stock fields:
$$
PS = \text{first\_nonmissing}(PS_{carry}, PS_{redeem}, PS_{liquid})
$$

Shareholders’ equity is defined by the priority rule
$$
SE =
\begin{cases}
SE_{total}, & \text{if available} \\
CEQ + PS, & \text{otherwise if available} \\
AT - LT, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Deferred taxes and investment tax credit is set to zero when missing:
$$
TXDITC^\* =
\begin{cases}
TXDITC, & \text{if available} \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Book equity is
$$
BE = SE + TXDITC^\* - PS
$$

Let $DecME_{t-12}$ denote the firm’s firm-year December market equity value observed at the calendar month exactly 12 months before $t$, and similarly for $t-17$. The two candidate ratios are
$$
BM^{(12)}_t =
\begin{cases}
\text{missing}, & \text{if } DecME_{t-12}=0 \\
\frac{BE_t}{DecME_{t-12}}, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$
$$
BM^{(17)}_t =
\begin{cases}
\text{missing}, & \text{if } DecME_{t-17}=0 \\
\frac{BE_t}{DecME_{t-17}}, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

The final signal is selected by calendar month:
$$
BMdec_t =
\begin{cases}
BM^{(12)}_t, & \text{if } month(t)\ge 6 \\
BM^{(17)}_t, & \text{if } month(t)< 6
\end{cases}
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a firm lacks a December price or shares observation in a given calendar year, the firm-year December market equity remains missing and the signal will be missing when that lag is required. If the lagged December market equity equals zero, the ratio is set to missing to avoid division by zero.

If total stockholders’ equity is missing, the construction falls back to common equity plus preferred stock, and then to assets minus liabilities. If preferred stock is missing in all preferred stock fields, it remains missing and can propagate to shareholders’ equity in the fallback branch that uses common equity plus preferred stock.

The lagging uses true calendar month offsets of 12 and 17 months, not row-based shifts. This ensures that missing months in the panel do not distort the intended timing convention.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly firm-level signal named BMdec. It is a floating-point ratio of book equity to lagged December market equity, with missing values when required inputs are missing or when the denominator is zero. The signal is aligned to the same firm-month availability timestamp used in the merged monthly panel.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix:
Price is taken in absolute value before computing market equity to neutralize signed price conventions. Shares outstanding is used as provided, so the market equity scale follows the native shares unit in the input.

The construction first assigns a December market equity within each firm-year, then retrieves that assigned value from 12 or 17 months earlier. This two-step approach implements the “use last December market equity” convention while respecting calendar time.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures how unusual a firm’s latest quarterly earnings are relative to its own recent earnings-change history. It computes an unexpected earnings component and standardizes it by the historical volatility of similar surprises, producing a unitless signal.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a firm identifier, a monthly availability timestamp, and quarterly basic earnings per share including extraordinary items. The earnings per share field is measured in USD per share for the quarter and may be affected by restatements and regime changes in extraordinary item reporting.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Align quarterly earnings per share observations to the month when they become available, and work within each firm’s time-ordered history. For each firm-month, locate the earnings per share from exactly 12 months earlier.

Compute a 12-month earnings change as the current quarterly earnings per share minus the value from 12 months earlier. This creates a year-over-year quarterly earnings growth proxy.

Construct a drift term by taking the simple average of the prior eight year-over-year earnings changes observed at 3-month intervals. These lags correspond to 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, and 24 months before the current availability month.

Compute the raw earnings surprise as the current year-over-year earnings change minus the drift term. This isolates the unexpected component relative to the firm’s recent pattern.

Estimate surprise volatility as the sample standard deviation of the prior eight raw earnings surprises at the same 3-month lag grid. Use a sample standard deviation with $ddof=1$ across the available lagged values.

Standardize the raw earnings surprise by dividing it by the estimated volatility. If the volatility is zero, the standardized value becomes infinite and is treated as missing.

Filter the output to keep only observations with a non-missing standardized value and a non-missing volatility estimate. Also remove observations where the volatility is extremely small, specifically not greater than $1\times 10^{-10}$.

Convert the availability timestamp to an integer year-month key of the form YYYYMM. Output the firm identifier, the YYYYMM key, and the standardized earnings surprise.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $t$ denote the month of availability for a given firm, and let $EPS_t$ be quarterly basic earnings per share including extraordinary items available at $t$.

Define the year-over-year earnings change as
$$
G_t = EPS_t - EPS_{t-12}.
$$

Define the drift component as the mean of the prior eight year-over-year changes sampled every three months:
$$
Drift_t = \frac{1}{8}\sum_{k\in\{3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24\}} G_{t-k}.
$$

Define the raw earnings surprise as
$$
ES^{raw}_t = G_t - Drift_t.
$$

Define the historical volatility of surprises as the sample standard deviation of the prior eight raw surprises:
$$
SD_t = \operatorname{StdDev}\Big(\{ES^{raw}_{t-k}\}_{k\in\{3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24\}}\Big),
$$
where the standard deviation uses $ddof=1$.

Define the standardized earnings surprise signal as
$$

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures how close the current month-end price is to the stock’s highest daily price observed over the prior 12 months. It implements the 52-week high ratio concept associated with George and Hwang (2004), computed as current price divided by the maximum price over the previous year.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a daily trading date field that identifies each trading day observation. It uses a daily price field that may be signed in the raw source and is converted to an absolute value before aggregation.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, map each daily trading date to its corresponding month period, represented by the month’s start timestamp. This month identifier is used to aggregate daily observations into monthly records.

Next, convert the daily price to an absolute value to remove sign conventions. This absolute daily price is the only price series used in subsequent steps.

Then, within each stock and month, compute two monthly summaries from daily data. One is the maximum absolute daily price in that month, and the other is the last available absolute daily price in that month.

After forming the monthly panel, sort observations by stock and month to prepare for time-series lagging. Create 12 lagged versions of the monthly maximum price, lagged by 1 through 12 months.

Compute the rolling 52-week high proxy as the maximum across those 12 lagged monthly maxima. This produces the highest monthly maximum observed in the prior 12 months, excluding the current month.

Finally, compute the signal as the ratio of the current month’s last available absolute price to the prior-12-month maximum. Store the resulting monthly value as the factor output.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $P_{d}$ be the signed daily price and let $A_{d} = |P_{d}|$ be the absolute daily price.

For stock $i$ and month $t$, define the within-month maximum and month-end price as:
$$
\text{MaxInMonth}_{i,t} = \max_{d \in t} A_{i,d}
$$
$$
\text{EndPrice}_{i,t} = A_{i,d^\ast(t)}
$$
where $d^\ast(t)$ is the last trading day in month $t$ with a non-missing price.

Define the prior-12-month high as the maximum of the previous 12 months’ within-month maxima:
$$
\text{HighPrior12}_{i,t} = \max\left(\text{MaxInMonth}_{i,t-1}, \text{MaxInMonth}_{i,t-2}, \ldots, \text{MaxInMonth}_{i,t-12}\right)
$$

The 52-week high ratio is:
$$
\text{High52}_{i,t} = \frac{\text{EndPrice}_{i,t}}{\text{HighPrior12}_{i,t}}
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If fewer than 12 prior months of monthly maxima exist for a stock, the prior-12-month high is taken over the available lags only. If no prior lagged maxima exist, the ratio is undefined.

If the prior-12-month high is missing or equals zero, the ratio is undefined due to division by missing or zero. If the current month-end price is missing, the ratio is also undefined.

The prior-12-month high excludes the current month by construction, because only lags 1 through 12 are used. The month-end price is the last observed trading-day price within the month, not a calendar month-end interpolation.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly stock-level predictor value representing the 52-week high ratio. Each record is indexed by stock identifier and month timestamp, and contains a single numeric field equal to the computed ratio.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The method uses absolute prices and does not apply split adjustments within this computation. Monthly aggregation uses the maximum daily absolute price for the month and the last available daily absolute price for the month.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures asset tangibility for manufacturing firms using a weighted balance-sheet composition of liquid and tangible asset components scaled by total assets. It is designed to proxy for the share of assets that are more pledgeable or collateral-like, consistent with the tangibility predictor used in related corporate finance research.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses firm identifiers and a monthly availability timestamp, plus balance-sheet items for cash and short-term investments, total receivables, total inventories, gross property, plant, and equipment, total assets, and an industry classification code. Cash and short-term investments, receivables, inventories, gross PP&E, and total assets are measured in currency units (millions of USD) as stock variables, and the industry code is treated as a numeric classification used for sample filtering.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the monthly panel of firm observations and ensure there is at most one record per firm and availability month. If multiple records exist for the same firm-month, keep the first encountered record.

Convert the industry classification code to a numeric value, treating non-numeric entries as missing. Restrict the sample to manufacturing firms by keeping only observations with industry codes between 2000 and 3999 inclusive.

Within each availability month, form deciles of total assets to support a financial-constraint indicator. Assign a decile rank from 1 (smallest) to 10 (largest), allowing fewer than 10 bins when ties prevent full decile formation.

Define a financial-constraint flag based on the size decile. Set the flag to 1 for the bottom three deciles and to 0 for the top three deciles, leaving the middle deciles unassigned.

Compute tangibility as a weighted sum of cash, receivables, inventories, and gross PP&E, divided by total assets. Drop observations where the resulting tangibility value is missing.

Convert the availability timestamp to an integer year-month key of the form YYYYMM. Output only the firm identifier, the year-month key, and the tangibility value.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
For each firm and availability month, tangibility is computed as
$$
\text{tangibility}=\frac{\text{cash} + 0.715\cdot \text{receivables} + 0.547\cdot \text{inventories} + 0.535\cdot \text{gross PP\&E}}{\text{total assets}}.
$$

The year-month output key is computed from the availability date as
$$
\text{YYYYMM}=100\cdot \text{year}(\text{availability date})+\text{month}(\text{availability date}).
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If the industry code cannot be parsed as numeric, the observation is excluded by the manufacturing filter. If total assets are missing, tangibility becomes missing and the observation is dropped; if total assets are zero, the division is undefined and should be treated as missing for consistency.

When forming size deciles within a month, insufficient unique total-asset values can reduce the number of bins; the decile rank is still assigned from the available bins. The financial-constraint flag is only defined for the smallest and largest size groups, and remains missing for the middle groups.

The factor is timestamped by the month of the availability date, and the output key reflects that month. The computation uses the first record per firm and availability month when duplicates exist, which can affect results if duplicates differ.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly firm-level file containing exactly three fields: a firm identifier, an integer year-month key in YYYYMM format, and a numeric tangibility value. Each row corresponds to one firm in one availability month, and tangibility is non-missing for all output rows.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Input item meanings: cash and short-term investments represent highly liquid cash-equivalent holdings; receivables are total current receivables; inventories are total inventories; gross PP&E is the gross book value of tangible fixed assets; total assets are the balance-sheet total. Tangibility is a constructed predictor defined by the stated weighted-asset formula and is restricted to manufacturing firms by industry code.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a stock’s systematic coskewness with the market, following Harvey and Siddique (2000). It estimates how the stock’s excess return co-moves with squared market excess returns using rolling sample moments over a 60-month window.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a stock’s monthly return including distributions and a monthly risk-free rate to form the stock’s excess return. It also uses the monthly market excess return to represent the market factor. The output is a monthly predictor value labeled Coskewness for each stock and month.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, align each stock-month with the same month’s market excess return and risk-free rate, and drop months where either market excess return or the risk-free rate is missing. Convert the stock return to an excess return by subtracting the risk-free rate. Keep the market series as the market excess return.

Next, define 60-month rolling windows for each stock, producing one window-ending month per calendar month. The implementation assigns each observation to exactly one of 60 interleaved “batches” so that each batch computes non-overlapping 60-month windows per stock. Each observation is mapped to the most recent window-ending month within its batch for that stock.

Within each stock and window-ending month, compute the sample mean of the stock excess return and the sample mean of the market excess return. Demean both series by subtracting their respective window means. These demeaned series are used to form the required second and cross moments.

Within each stock and window-ending month, compute the average of the product of demeaned stock excess return and squared demeaned market excess return. Also compute the average squared demeaned stock excess return and the average squared demeaned market excess return. Combine these moments into a normalized coskewness ratio.

Finally, require at least 12 monthly observations within the window to report a value. Convert the internal month index back to a calendar year-month identifier and output the coskewness value for each stock-month. Sort the final output by stock identifier and month.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $r_{i,t}$ be the stock’s monthly return and $r_{f,t}$ be the monthly risk-free rate. Define the stock’s excess return as $$x_{i,t} = r_{i,t} - r_{f,t}.$$ Let $m_t$ be the market excess return.

For a given stock $i$ and a given window-ending month $T$, consider the set of months $t$ in the 60-month window ending at $T$. Define window means $$\bar{x}_{i,T} = \frac{1}{N_{i,T}}\sum_{t \in W_{i,T}} x_{i,t}, \quad \bar{m}_T = \frac{1}{N_{i,T}}\sum_{t \in W_{i,T}} m_t,$$ where $N_{i,T}$ is the number of available months in the window.

Define demeaned series $$\tilde{x}_{i,t} = x_{i,t} - \bar{x}_{i,T}, \quad \tilde{m}_t = m_t - \bar{m}_T.$$ Define sample moments $$E[\tilde{x}^2]_{i,T} = \frac{1}{N_{i,T}}\sum_{t \in W_{i,T}} \tilde{x}_{i,t}^2,$$ $$E[\tilde{m}^2]_{i,T} = \frac{1}{N_{i,T}}\sum_{t \in W_{i,T}} \tilde{m}_t^2,$$ $$E[\tilde{x}\tilde{m}^2]_{i,T} = \frac{1}{N_{i,T}}\sum_{t \in W_{i,T}} \tilde{x}_{i,t}\tilde{m}_t^2.$$

The reported coskewness is $$\mathrm{Coskewness}_{i,T} = \frac{E[\tilde{x}\tilde{m}^2]_{i,T}}{\sqrt{E[\tilde{x}^2]_{i,T}} \cdot E[\tilde{m}^2]_{i,T}}.$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If the market excess return or the risk-free rate is missing for a month, that month is excluded before any window construction. If fewer than 12 observations are available for a stock in a given 60-month window, the factor value for that stock and window-ending month is not produced.

If $E[\tilde{x}^2]_{i,T}=0$ or $E[\tilde{m}^2]_{i,T}=0$, the normalization would be undefined; the implementation does not add an explicit safeguard beyond the data and window requirements. The factor is timestamped to the window-ending month $T$ and uses information from that month and the preceding months within the 60-month window.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel keyed by stock identifier and a year-month integer in the form YYYYMM. For each key, the output contains a single numeric value named Coskewness computed as the normalized coskewness ratio above. The output is sorted by stock identifier and then by YYYYMM in ascending order.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The 60-month windowing is implemented via an interleaving scheme that assigns each month to one of 60 groups and then forward-fills the most recent group month within each stock. This produces one computed value per stock per calendar month while keeping each batch’s windows non-overlapping. The demeaning and moment calculations are performed within each stock and window-ending month group, using simple averages over the available observations.

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

base_path = Path("../pyData")
intermediate_path = base_path / "Intermediate"
predictors_path = base_path / "Predictors"
predictors_path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

monthly_crsp = pl.read_parquet(intermediate_path / "monthlyCRSP.parquet")

monthly_ff = pl.read_parquet(intermediate_path / "monthlyFF.parquet")

merged_data = monthly_crsp.join(
    monthly_ff.select(["time_avail_m", "mktrf", "rf"]), on="time_avail_m", how="inner"
).filter(pl.col("mktrf").is_not_null() & pl.col("rf").is_not_null())

merged_data = merged_data.with_columns(
    [pl.col("mktrf").alias("mkt"), (pl.col("ret") - pl.col("rf")).alias("ret")]
).drop(["rf", "mktrf"])

merged_data = merged_data.sort(["permno", "time_avail_m"], descending=[False, True])

merged_data = merged_data.with_columns(
    [
        (
            (pl.col("time_avail_m").dt.year() - 1960) * 12
            + (pl.col("time_avail_m").dt.month() - 1)
        ).alias("time_avail_m_int"),
    ]
).with_columns([(pl.col("time_avail_m_int") % 60).alias("m60")])

batch_results = []

for m in range(60):

    batch_df = merged_data.clone()

    batch_df = batch_df.with_columns(
        [
            pl.when(pl.col("m60") != m)
            .then(None)
            .otherwise(pl.col("time_avail_m_int"))
            .alias("time_avail_m_batch")
        ]
    )

    batch_df = batch_df.with_columns(
        [
            pl.col("time_avail_m_batch")
            .forward_fill()
            .over("permno")
            .alias("time_avail_m_filled")
        ]
    )

    batch_df = batch_df.filter(pl.col("time_avail_m_filled").is_not_null())

    batch_df = batch_df.drop(["time_avail_m", "time_avail_m_int", "m60"])

    means_df = batch_df.group_by(["permno", "time_avail_m_filled"]).agg(
        [pl.col("ret").mean().alias("E_ret"), pl.col("mkt").mean().alias("E_mkt")]
    )

    batch_df = batch_df.join(
        means_df, on=["permno", "time_avail_m_filled"], how="inner"
    )
    batch_df = batch_df.with_columns(
        [
            (pl.col("ret") - pl.col("E_ret")).alias("ret_demeaned"),
            (pl.col("mkt") - pl.col("E_mkt")).alias("mkt_demeaned"),
        ]
    ).drop(["E_ret", "E_mkt"])

    batch_df = batch_df.with_columns(
        [
            pl.col("ret_demeaned").pow(2).alias("ret2"),
            pl.col("mkt_demeaned").pow(2).alias("mkt2"),
            (pl.col("ret_demeaned") * pl.col("mkt_demeaned").pow(2)).alias("ret_mkt2"),
        ]
    )

    coskew_df = batch_df.group_by(["permno", "time_avail_m_filled"]).agg(
        [
            pl.col("ret_mkt2").mean().alias("E_ret_mkt2"),
            pl.col("ret2").mean().alias("E_ret2"),
            pl.col("mkt2").mean().alias("E_mkt2"),
            pl.col("ret_demeaned")
            .count()
            .alias("nobs"),  # Count observations for minimum requirement
        ]
    )

    coskew_df = coskew_df.with_columns(
        [
            (pl.col("E_ret_mkt2") / (pl.col("E_ret2").sqrt() * pl.col("E_mkt2"))).alias(
                "Coskewness"
            )
        ]
    )

    coskew_df = coskew_df.filter(pl.col("nobs") >= 12)

    batch_result = coskew_df.select(
        [
            pl.col("permno"),
            pl.col("time_avail_m_filled").alias("time_avail_m"),
            pl.col("Coskewness"),
        ]
    )

    batch_results.append(batch_result)

final_result = pl.concat(batch_results)

final_result = (
    final_result.with_columns(
        [
            (1960 + pl.col("time_avail_m") // 12).cast(pl.Int64).alias("yyyy"),
            (pl.col("time_avail_m") % 12 + 1).cast(pl.Int64).alias("mm"),
        ]
    )
    .with_columns([(pl.col("yyyy") * 100 + pl.col("mm")).alias("yyyymm")])
    .select(["permno", "yyyymm", "Coskewness"])
)

final_result = final_result.sort(["permno", "yyyymm"])

final_result.write_csv(predictors_path / "Coskewness.csv")

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures profitability relative to shareholders’ book equity by scaling net income by common equity. It is intended to capture how efficiently a firm generates earnings from the book value attributable to common shareholders.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a monthly-availability panel that contains firm identifiers, a monthly availability timestamp, net income, and common equity. Net income is bottom-line net income after extraordinary items and discontinued operations attributable to the company, measured in millions of USD and reported at an annual frequency. Common equity is the book value of equity available to common shareholders, measured in millions of USD and reported at an annual frequency.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, within each firm and monthly availability timestamp, retain only the first record when duplicates exist. This ensures a single observation per firm per availability month.

Next, compute the signal as net income divided by common equity. The result is a dimensionless ratio.

Then, remove observations where the computed ratio is missing. Only non-missing signal values are kept.

Finally, convert the monthly availability timestamp into an integer year-month key of the form $yyyymm$. Keep only the firm identifier, the year-month key, and the computed signal.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
The factor is defined as:
$$
\mathrm{RoE} = \frac{\mathrm{Net\ Income}}{\mathrm{Common\ Equity}}
$$

The year-month key is constructed from the availability date as:
$$
yyyymm = 100 \times \mathrm{year}(\mathrm{availability\ date}) + \mathrm{month}(\mathrm{availability\ date})
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If multiple records exist for the same firm and availability month, only the first encountered record is used, and the rest are ignored. This choice can affect results if duplicates differ due to restatements or data merges.

If common equity equals zero, the ratio becomes undefined or infinite depending on the data representation. Such cases are not explicitly filtered unless they appear as missing after computation.

The signal is timestamped by the month in which the accounting data are available, not the fiscal period end date. This aligns the factor with an availability-based timing convention to reduce look-ahead bias.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel keyed by firm identifier and $yyyymm$. It contains a single column for the factor value named RoE, with rows restricted to non-missing RoE values.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Net income may include extraordinary items and discontinued operations, and it is subject to restatements; alternative earnings definitions may behave differently. Common equity can be affected by preferred stock and complex equity structures, so it may not match simpler equity constructions in all cases.

factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction requires a monthly stock return series and a monthly time index that indicates when each return observation becomes available for use. The monthly stock return is a decimal total return for the month, typically including distributions, and may reflect special handling of delistings depending on the upstream return definition. factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:

Start from the monthly panel and keep only one observation per firm per month, retaining the first occurrence when duplicates exist. Then sort the panel by firm and month to ensure lags are computed on a properly ordered time series.

Compute operating assets as total assets minus cash and short-term investments. Compute operating liabilities as total assets minus long-term debt, minority interest, deferred charges, and common equity.

Within each firm, compute lagged total assets as the value of total assets from twelve months earlier. Compute net operating assets as operating assets minus operating liabilities, divided by lagged total assets.

factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a firm identifier, a monthly availability timestamp, total assets, and total inventories. Total assets are the balance-sheet total assets item, reported in currency units (millions of USD). Total inventories are the balance-sheet total inventories item, reported in currency units (millions of USD). The output is a monthly predictor value labeled as Inventory Growth.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the panel containing firm identifier, monthly availability timestamp, total assets, and total inventories. If multiple rows share the same firm and timestamp, keep only the first and discard the rest.

Sort observations by firm and timestamp to ensure lags align correctly. Within each firm, compute 12-month lags for total inventories and total assets.

Compute the 12-month change in inventories and scale it by the average of current and 12-month-lagged total assets. This produces a size-adjusted inventory growth measure.

Keep only the firm identifier, timestamp, and the computed signal, and drop rows where the signal is missing. Convert the timestamp into an integer year-month key of the form $YYYYMM$, then output the firm identifier, $YYYYMM$, and the signal.

Let $t$ denote the monthly availability timestamp for a given firm. Define the 12-month lag operator as $x_{t-12}$.

Inventory Growth is computed as:
$$
\text{Inventory Growth}_t
=
\frac{\text{Inventories}_t - \text{Inventories}_{t-12}}
{\left(\text{Total Assets}_t + \text{Total Assets}_{t-12}\right)/2}
$$

The year-month key is computed from the timestamp as:
$$

$$

If a firm lacks a valid 12-month lag for inventories or total assets, the signal is missing and the observation is removed. If total assets are missing at $t$ or $t-12$, the signal is missing and removed.

factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel with one row per firm and $YYYYMM$ where the signal is defined. Fields are the firm identifier, $YYYYMM$ as an integer, and the Inventory Growth signal as a numeric value. Rows with missing signal values are excluded.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Total assets are defined as the balance-sheet total assets item and may be affected by restatements and acquisition accounting. Total inventories are defined as total inventories and may be influenced by inventory accounting methods such as LIFO or FIFO. The signal is a constructed predictor and should be interpreted as a scaled 12-month inventory change.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures the year-over-year change in quarterly total income tax expense, scaled by total assets from one year earlier. It is intended to capture changes in firms’ tax expense intensity relative to their prior-year balance sheet size.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a monthly security-to-firm mapping with a monthly availability timestamp and total assets, and a quarterly firm dataset with the same monthly availability timestamp and quarterly total income tax expense. factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
First, align the monthly total assets data with the quarterly tax expense data by matching on firm identifier and the monthly availability timestamp. Keep only observations present in both sources at the same availability month.

Next, within each firm, create a lagged availability timestamp equal to 12 months before the current availability month. This lag is calendar-based, not a fixed number of rows.

Then, obtain the tax expense value from exactly 12 months earlier by matching the firm identifier and the lagged availability timestamp to the earlier tax expense observation. Store this as the 12-month lag of quarterly tax expense.

Similarly, obtain total assets from exactly 12 months earlier by matching the firm identifier and the lagged availability timestamp to the earlier total assets observation. Store this as the 12-month lag of total assets.

Finally, compute the signal as the difference between current quarterly tax expense and its 12-month lag, divided by the 12-month lag of total assets. The resulting value is the monthly signal for that availability month.

Let $t$ denote the monthly availability timestamp for a firm, and let $t-12$ denote the timestamp exactly 12 months earlier.

Let $\mathrm{TaxExp}_t$ be quarterly total income tax expense available at $t$, and let $\mathrm{Assets}_{t-12}$ be total assets available at $t-12$.

$$

factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:

factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly predictor named ChTax, defined for each security-month where the firm has both current aligned inputs and valid 12-month lagged inputs. factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Total assets can be affected by restatements and acquisition accounting, which may change the scaling base across time. Quarterly total income tax expense includes both current and deferred components and may be volatile due to one-time items, valuation allowances, or jurisdictional mix changes.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: The factor measures how unusual a firm’s current quarterly revenue per share change is relative to its own recent history. It is designed to capture revenue “surprises” after removing a simple drift component and then scaling by the firm’s historical surprise volatility.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a firm identifier, a monthly availability timestamp, quarterly total revenue, and quarterly common shares reserved for conversion. The output is a monthly signal value aligned to the availability month.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the master panel of firm identifiers and monthly availability timestamps, and keep only rows with a valid firm accounting key. Join in quarterly accounting fields on the accounting key and the same availability timestamp, keeping only matched rows. Sort observations by firm and availability time to support time-based self-joins.

Compute revenue per share as quarterly total revenue divided by quarterly common shares reserved for conversion. Create a 12-month calendar lag of the availability timestamp and self-join within firm to fetch revenue per share from exactly 12 months earlier. Compute the year-over-year change in revenue per share as current revenue per share minus the 12-month-lagged value.

Construct a drift estimate using calendar-based lags of the year-over-year change. For each lag in months $n \in \{3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24\}$, self-join within firm on the timestamp shifted back by $n$ months to retrieve the lagged year-over-year change. Take the simple mean across the available lagged values to form the drift.

Compute the raw revenue surprise as the current year-over-year change minus the drift. Then build a volatility estimate by repeating the same lag-and-join procedure on the raw revenue surprise for the same set of lags. Compute the sample standard deviation across the available lagged surprises using an $n-1$ denominator.

Standardize the raw revenue surprise by dividing by the historical standard deviation. Replace infinite standardized values with missing values, which can occur when the standard deviation is zero. Keep only observations with a non-missing standardized value and a reliable, strictly positive standard deviation above a very small threshold.

Finally, convert the availability timestamp to an integer year-month format and retain only the firm identifier, year-month, and standardized revenue surprise. Cast the firm identifier and year-month to integers for the final output.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Revenue per share is
$$
\text{revps}_t = \frac{\text{revtq}_t}{\text{cshprq}_t}.
$$

The year-over-year change in revenue per share is
$$
\text{GrTemp}_t = \text{revps}_t - \text{revps}_{t-12m}.
$$

The drift is the mean of calendar-lagged year-over-year changes over $n \in \{3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24\}$ months:
$$
\text{Drift}_t = \frac{1}{K_t}\sum_{n \in \mathcal{N}} \text{GrTemp}_{t-nm},
\quad \mathcal{N}=\{3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24\},
$$
where $K_t$ is the number of non-missing lagged terms available at time $t$.

The raw revenue surprise is
$$
\text{RSraw}_t = \text{GrTemp}_t - \text{Drift}_t.
$$

The historical volatility is the sample standard deviation of lagged raw surprises:
$$
\text{SD}_t = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K_t-1}\sum_{n \in \mathcal{N}}\left(\text{RSraw}_{t-nm}-\overline{\text{RSraw}}_t\right)^2},
$$
where $\overline{\text{RSraw}}_t$ is the mean of the available lagged raw surprises and $K_t$ is their count.

The standardized revenue surprise is
$$
\text{RevenueSurprise}_t = \frac{\text{RSraw}_t}{\text{SD}_t}.
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
Calendar-based lags require an exact match on the availability timestamp shifted by a whole number of months; if a lagged timestamp is absent, that lag contributes as missing. The drift and volatility calculations use the mean and sample standard deviation across available lags, so they can be computed with partial history, but the standard deviation is missing when fewer than two lagged surprises exist.

If common shares reserved for conversion is zero or missing, revenue per share becomes undefined and will propagate to missing downstream values. If the historical standard deviation is zero or extremely small, standardization can create infinite or unstable values; infinities are set to missing and observations with $\text{SD} \le 10^{-8}$ are removed. The signal is timestamped to the month of the availability date used in the joins, and the final year-month is derived directly from that availability timestamp.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel keyed by firm identifier and integer year-month, containing a single numeric column for the standardized revenue surprise. Rows are included only when the standardized value is finite and the historical standard deviation is non-missing and greater than $10^{-8}$. The signal is intended to be interpreted as a z-scored surprise, where larger positive values indicate unusually strong revenue-per-share changes relative to the firm’s recent history.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Quarterly total revenue is a flow measure of operating revenue for the quarter, typically close to net sales for industrial firms. Common shares reserved for conversion is a potential-dilution share count with patchy coverage, and it is used here as the scaling denominator for revenue per share. The constructed signal is monthly because it is aligned to the monthly availability timestamp, even though it is built from quarterly accounting inputs.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a stock’s intermediate-term momentum by compounding its past monthly returns over the prior 11 months and excluding the current month. It is intended to align with the 12-month momentum construction associated with the Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) momentum framework, using a skip of month $t$.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses a monthly stock return series and a monthly time index for each security identifier. The return input is the stock’s monthly total return expressed in decimal form, and the output is a monthly predictor value representing 12-month momentum.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from a panel of monthly observations keyed by security identifier and monthly availability time. Keep only the identifier, the monthly time field, and the monthly return.

Within each security, sort observations in ascending monthly time. Replace missing monthly returns with $0$ before any lagging or compounding.

Create calendar-aware monthly lags of the return for lags $1$ through $11$. Each lag must refer to the prior calendar month(s) for that same security, not merely the prior row.

Compute momentum at month $t$ by compounding the lagged returns from $t-1$ through $t-11$ and subtracting $1$. This construction excludes the current month’s return at $t$.

Return only the security identifier, the monthly time field, and the computed momentum value. Save the resulting monthly predictor under the factor name.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $r_{i,t}$ be the monthly return for security $i$ at month $t$, after replacing missing values with $0$. Define the $k$-month lagged return as $r_{i,t-k}$ using a calendar-aware monthly lag.

The factor value is
$$
\mathrm{Mom12m}_{i,t}=\left(\prod_{k=1}^{11}\left(1+r_{i,t-k}\right)\right)-1.
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a monthly return is missing, it is treated as $0$ for purposes of the product, which makes the corresponding term $(1+0)=1$. If a lagged month does not exist for a security due to insufficient history or a gap in monthly observations, the lag value will be missing and the compounded momentum will consequently be missing.

The signal at month $t$ uses only information from months $t-1$ through $t-11$. The current month’s return $r_{i,t}$ is not used, ensuring a one-month skip relative to the formation month.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly panel with one row per security and month where the factor is defined. It contains the security identifier, the monthly time field, and a single numeric column named Mom12m representing the compounded prior-11-month return minus one.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The return input is a monthly total return series in decimal units, and the factor output is a constructed monthly predictor. The construction follows a multiplicative compounding of lagged monthly returns and implements missing-return handling by zero-imputation prior to lag creation.

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a firm’s cash flow relative to its equity market value, following the cash-flow-to-price style metric used in Lakonishok, Shleifer, and Vishny (1994). It is intended to capture “cheapness” based on cash-flow generation scaled by market equity.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses income before extraordinary items and depreciation expense, each expressed as an annual flow measure in millions of USD. It also uses monthly market equity for the firm, aligned to the same monthly availability timestamp as the accounting data.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the monthly accounting panel and keep only the firm identifier, security identifier, monthly availability timestamp, and the two accounting fields. If multiple records exist for the same security and month, keep the first and discard the rest.

Join the monthly market equity series to the accounting panel using the security identifier and the monthly availability timestamp. The join keeps every market-equity month, even when accounting fields are missing.

Compute cash flow as the sum of income before extraordinary items and depreciation. This sum is computed only where the underlying components are present; otherwise it remains missing.

Compute the factor as cash flow divided by market equity. If market equity equals zero, set the factor to missing to avoid division by zero.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Cash flow is defined as:
$$
\text{cash\_flow} = \text{income} + \text{depreciation}
$$

Cash flow to market is defined as:
$$
\text{CF} =
\begin{cases}
\frac{\text{cash\_flow}}{\text{market\_equity}}, & \text{if } \text{market\_equity} \neq 0 \\
\text{missing}, & \text{if } \text{market\_equity} = 0
\end{cases}
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If either income or depreciation is missing for a given month, cash flow is missing and the factor is missing. If market equity is missing, the factor is missing.

If market equity is exactly zero, the factor is set to missing rather than infinite or undefined. Duplicate security-month accounting observations are resolved by keeping the first occurrence.

The factor is produced at the monthly availability timestamp used to align accounting data with market equity. Months that exist in the market-equity series but lack accounting data are retained with a missing factor value.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly predictor named CF. It is indexed by security identifier and monthly availability timestamp, and contains a single numeric value per security-month representing cash flow to market equity, or missing when not computable.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix:
Income before extraordinary items is an annual flow measure reflecting bottom-line profitability before extraordinary and discontinued items, and may be restated over time. Depreciation is an annual flow measure that may sometimes reflect combined depreciation and amortization depending on reporting.

This factor is a constructed monthly signal derived from annual accounting flows aligned to monthly availability and scaled by monthly market equity. The construction explicitly treats zero market equity as an invalid denominator and returns missing in that case.

factor_logic_in_paper.factor_name: Taxable income to income ratio (Lev and Nissim style)
factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor proxies for taxable income relative to accounting income by scaling current tax expense by the statutory top corporate tax rate and dividing by income before extraordinary items. It is designed to match the Lev and Nissim (2004) taxable-income-to-income construction while reproducing specific missing-data and nonpositive-income handling.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction uses income taxes paid on foreign current income and income taxes paid on U.S. federal current income, both measured as annual income statement flows. It also uses total income tax expense and deferred tax expense from the income statement, plus income before extraordinary items as the income denominator. The observation timestamp is the monthly availability date used to assign a calendar year for the statutory rate and to produce a year-month output key.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from one record per firm and monthly availability date, keeping the first available observation when duplicates exist. Extract the calendar year from the availability date to select the applicable statutory top corporate tax rate.

Assign the statutory rate as a piecewise constant by year: $0.48$ by default, $0.46$ for 1979–1986, $0.40$ for 1987, $0.34$ for 1988–1992, and $0.35$ for 1993 onward. This rate is used to convert current tax expense into an implied taxable income measure.

Compute the baseline ratio using current taxes as the sum of foreign current and federal current taxes. Convert that current tax sum into implied taxable income by dividing by the statutory rate, then divide by income before extraordinary items.

If either the foreign current tax or the federal current tax is missing, replace the baseline ratio with an alternative ratio based on total tax expense net of deferred tax expense. Specifically, use total tax expense minus deferred tax expense as a proxy for current tax expense, then apply the same statutory-rate scaling and income division.

Handle the division-by-zero case before other nonpositive-income rules. When income before extraordinary items equals zero and there is any nonzero reported tax activity in any of the tax fields, set the factor value to $1$.

After the baseline and alternative computations, if the factor value is still missing and income before extraordinary items is nonpositive, set the factor value to $1$. This acts as a conservative imputation when losses or zero income coincide with tax activity patterns that would otherwise be undefined.

Apply an additional nonpositive-income rule intended to mimic common statistical-software missing-value logic for tax activity. When income before extraordinary items is nonpositive and either current taxes are positive (treating a missing federal component as not blocking a positive foreign component), or total tax expense exceeds deferred tax expense, set the factor value to $1$.

Also treat the case where both current-tax components are missing but there is nonzero activity in total tax expense or deferred tax expense, combined with nonpositive income. In that situation, set the factor value to $1$ to reflect tax activity despite missing current-tax detail.

Convert the availability date to a year-month integer key of the form YYYYMM. Finally, keep only finite factor values by dropping missing and non-finite results, and output only the firm identifier, the year-month key, and the factor.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $t$ denote the monthly availability date and let $y$ be its calendar year. Define the statutory top corporate tax rate $tr(y)$ as
$$
tr(y)=
\begin{cases}
0.46, & 1979 \le y \le 1986 \\
0.40, & y = 1987 \\
0.34, & 1988 \le y \le 1992 \\
0.35, & y \ge 1993 \\
0.48, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Define the baseline taxable-income-to-income ratio as
$$
Tax = \frac{\frac{txfo + txfed}{tr(y)}}{ib}.
$$

When either current-tax component is missing, replace it with the alternative ratio
$$
Tax = \frac{\frac{txt - txdi}{tr(y)}}{ib}.
$$

For the year-month key, define
$$
yyyymm = 100 \cdot \text{year}(t) + \text{month}(t).
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If $ib=0$ and any of the tax fields indicates nonzero activity, the factor is forced to $1$ to avoid undefined division while preserving the presence of tax activity. If $ib \le 0$ and the computed ratio is missing, the factor is set to $1$, and it is also set to $1$ under specific tax-activity conditions that treat missing current-tax components in a permissive way. Observations with missing or non-finite final factor values are removed rather than imputed further.

The factor is timestamped by the monthly availability date, and the statutory rate is chosen using the calendar year of that availability date. The output is indexed by the derived YYYYMM key corresponding to that same availability month.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly predictor value named Tax, representing taxable income to income. Each row contains a firm identifier, a YYYYMM integer time key, and a finite numeric Tax value. Rows with missing or infinite Tax are excluded from the delivered output.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The construction interprets current tax expense as either the sum of foreign and federal current taxes when both are present, or as total tax expense net of deferred tax expense when either current component is missing. The nonpositive-income overrides set the ratio to $1$ in several cases to emulate legacy missing-value behavior and to ensure a defined signal when tax activity exists but the income denominator is zero or nonpositive.

df = pd.read_parquet(
    "../pyData/Intermediate/m_aCompustat.parquet",
    columns=["permno", "time_avail_m", "txfo", "txfed", "ib", "txt", "txdi"],
)

df = df.groupby(["permno", "time_avail_m"]).first().reset_index()

df["year"] = df["time_avail_m"].dt.year

df["tr"] = 0.48  # Default rate
df.loc[(df["year"] >= 1979) & (df["year"] <= 1986), "tr"] = 0.46
df.loc[df["year"] == 1987, "tr"] = 0.4
df.loc[(df["year"] >= 1988) & (df["year"] <= 1992), "tr"] = 0.34
df.loc[df["year"] >= 1993, "tr"] = 0.35

df["Tax"] = ((df["txfo"] + df["txfed"]) / df["tr"]) / df["ib"]

condition_missing = df["txfo"].isna() | df["txfed"].isna()
df.loc[condition_missing, "Tax"] = ((df["txt"] - df["txdi"]) / df["tr"]) / df["ib"]

div_by_zero = (df["ib"] == 0) & (
    (df["txfo"].notna() & (df["txfo"] != 0))
    | (df["txfed"].notna() & (df["txfed"] != 0))
    | (df["txt"].notna() & (df["txt"] != 0))
    | (df["txdi"].notna() & (df["txdi"] != 0))
)
df.loc[div_by_zero, "Tax"] = 1.0

cond_step3_simple = df["Tax"].isna() & (df["ib"] <= 0).fillna(False)
df.loc[cond_step3_simple, "Tax"] = 1.0

cond_txfo_txfed_fixed = (df["txfed"].isna() & (df["txfo"] > 0).fillna(False)) | (
    ~df["txfed"].isna() & (df["txfo"] + df["txfed"] > 0).fillna(False)
)
cond_txt_txdi = (df["txt"] > df["txdi"]).fillna(False)

cond_both_missing = (
    df["txfo"].isna()
    & df["txfed"].isna()
    & (
        (df["txt"].notna() & (df["txt"] != 0))
        | (df["txdi"].notna() & (df["txdi"] != 0))
    )
    & (df["ib"] <= 0).fillna(False)
)

cond_standard = (cond_txfo_txfed_fixed | cond_txt_txdi | cond_both_missing) & (
    df["ib"] <= 0
).fillna(False)
df.loc[cond_standard, "Tax"] = 1.0

df["yyyymm"] = df["time_avail_m"].dt.year * 100 + df["time_avail_m"].dt.month

df = df[df["Tax"].notna() & np.isfinite(df["Tax"])].copy()

df = df[["permno", "yyyymm", "Tax"]].copy()

factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a firm’s accumulated R&D “capital” relative to its total assets by applying declining weights to current and past R&D expenditures. It is designed to be used only within the smallest size group each month, matching the “small firms only” restriction.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction uses total assets and R&D expense from a monthly fundamentals panel, and market equity from a monthly master panel used only to form size groups. Total assets are the firm’s reported balance-sheet total assets, and market equity is the stock-level market capitalization used for monthly size sorting. R&D expense is treated as missing-at-random and is set to zero when absent.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from a monthly firm panel containing total assets and R&D expense, and remove any duplicate firm-month records. Merge in the same-month market equity needed for size sorting.

Fill gaps in the monthly time series so each firm has a continuous monthly calendar before creating lags. Replace missing R&D expense with zero to form the working R&D series.

Create calendar-based lags of the working R&D series at 12, 24, 36, and 48 months. These lags must align by month, not by row order.

Compute R&D capital as a weighted sum of current and lagged R&D, then scale by total assets. The weights decline linearly in steps of 0.2 from the current value to the 48-month lag.

Set the factor to missing for any month earlier than calendar year 1980. This restriction is applied after the ratio is computed.

Within each month, sort firms into three size groups using market equity and assign group labels from 1 to 3. Keep the factor only for group 1, and set it to missing for groups 2 and 3.

If a firm cannot be assigned to a size group in a given month, set the factor to missing for that firm-month. The final saved signal is the small-firm-only R&D capital-to-assets value.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $X_t$ be current-month R&D expense after replacing missing values with zero, and let $A_t$ be current-month total assets.

Define the weighted R&D capital stock numerator as:
$$
K_t = X_t + 0.8X_{t-12} + 0.6X_{t-24} + 0.4X_{t-36} + 0.2X_{t-48}.
$$

The factor value is:
$$
RDcap_t = \frac{K_t}{A_t}.
$$

The factor is only retained when the firm is in the smallest monthly size tertile:
$$
RDcap_t =
\begin{cases}
\frac{K_t}{A_t}, & \text{if size\_tertile}_t = 1 \text{ and year}(t)\ge 1980 \\
\text{missing}, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If total assets are missing in a month, the ratio is undefined and the factor should be missing. If total assets are zero, the ratio is not meaningful and should be treated as missing to avoid infinite values.

If lagged R&D values are unavailable due to insufficient history, the weighted sum will be partially missing unless the lagging procedure yields missing values; the implementation should follow the lag outputs as constructed. The pre-1980 exclusion forces missing values regardless of available history.

Size tertiles are formed independently each month using available market equity values, and the factor is then filtered to the smallest tertile. If the monthly tertile assignment fails for a firm due to missing market equity or insufficient distinct values, the factor is set to missing.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly firm-level signal equal to R&D capital-to-assets, available only for firms in the smallest monthly size tertile and only from 1980 onward. The signal is missing for all other firm-months, including those without a valid size assignment. The saved field name is RDcap.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Total assets are balance-sheet total assets and may be affected by restatements and acquisition accounting. Market equity is the stock-level market capitalization used for sorting and may depend on the underlying size construction conventions. The factor follows a five-year (0 to 48 months) declining-weight accumulation of R&D expense, with missing R&D treated as zero before lagging and accumulation.

factor_logic_in_paper.factor_name: Predicted dividend yield (frequency-adjusted lag), transformed into a monthly tercile signal.
factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: The factor estimates a one-month-ahead dividend yield by forecasting the next dividend amount using a lag that depends on the firm’s dividend payment frequency. It then converts the predicted yield into a cross-sectional, month-by-month ordinal signal intended to be comparable across firms.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The construction uses distribution event records containing a firm identifier, three distribution classification codes, a per-share distribution amount, and an ex-distribution date. It also uses a monthly master file containing the firm identifier, a month timestamp, and the month’s price. It additionally merges monthly return and ex-dividend return fields for the same firm-month, although these merged return fields are not used in the final signal. The output is written as a firm-by-month table containing the final signal value.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Filter distribution events to a specific distribution type by keeping only records with the primary code equal to 1 and the secondary code equal to 2. Further restrict to events whose tertiary code is in the set $\{3,4,5\}$. Convert the ex-distribution date to a month timestamp and drop events missing either the month timestamp or the distribution amount.

Aggregate distribution amounts to the firm-month level by summing the per-share distribution amount within each firm, tertiary code, and month. If multiple tertiary codes occur in the same firm-month, keep only the first after sorting by firm, month, and tertiary code. This yields a single firm-month distribution amount and an associated tertiary code.

Merge the firm-month distribution data into the monthly master file by firm and month, retaining all firm-months from the master file. Merge monthly return fields by firm and month as well, even though they do not affect subsequent calculations. Sort observations by firm and month.

Within each firm, forward-fill the tertiary code across months to carry the most recently observed frequency classification. Replace missing firm-month distribution amounts with zero. Compute a trailing 12-month sum of the firm-month distribution amount, using up to 12 months and allowing shorter histories.

Keep only firm-months with a strictly positive trailing 12-month distribution sum. Initialize the predicted next dividend amount as missing. Assign the predicted next dividend amount using a frequency-specific lag of the firm-month distribution amount.

Treat firms as quarterly payers when the carried-forward tertiary code indicates quarterly behavior or is missing, and set the predicted next dividend amount to the distribution amount from two months earlier. Treat firms as semiannual payers when the tertiary code indicates semiannual behavior, and set the predicted next dividend amount to the distribution amount from five months earlier. Treat firms as annual payers when the tertiary code indicates annual behavior, and set the predicted next dividend amount to the distribution amount from eleven months earlier.

Compute the predicted dividend yield as the predicted next dividend amount divided by the absolute value of price. Set negative or zero predicted yields aside for ranking by keeping only strictly positive predicted yields. Within each month, assign firms with positive predicted yields into three quantile bins, producing labels 1 through 3.

Override the quantile label to 0 when the predicted dividend yield equals exactly zero. Drop firm-months where the quantile label is missing. Convert the month timestamp to an integer year-month key and output the firm identifier, year-month key, and the final signal value.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $D_{i,t}$ be the firm-month distribution amount after aggregation and zero-filling, and let $P_{i,t}$ be the monthly price.

The trailing 12-month distribution sum is
$$
D12_{i,t}=\sum_{k=0}^{11} D_{i,t-k}.
$$

The predicted next dividend amount $Ediv1_{i,t}$ is defined by the carried-forward frequency class:
$$
Ediv1_{i,t}=
\begin{cases}
D_{i,t-2}, & \text{quarterly or unknown frequency} \\
D_{i,t-5}, & \text{semiannual frequency} \\
D_{i,t-11}, & \text{annual frequency}.
\end{cases}
$$

The predicted dividend yield is
$$
Edy1_{i,t}=\frac{Ediv1_{i,t}}{|P_{i,t}|}.
$$

Define the positive-yield subset as $Edy1pos_{i,t}=Edy1_{i,t}$ if $Edy1_{i,t}>0$, otherwise missing. The final signal is a month-by-month tercile rank of $Edy1pos_{i,t}$ labeled in $\{1,2,3\}$, with an override to 0 when $Edy1_{i,t}=0$.
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a firm has no distribution events in a month, its firm-month distribution amount is set to zero, but it can still be retained if its trailing 12-month sum remains positive. If the firm lacks sufficient history for the required lag, the predicted next dividend amount becomes missing and the firm-month will not receive a quantile label.

If multiple distribution types occur within the same firm-month, only one is retained after sorting, which can discard additional same-month distributions. If price is missing, the predicted yield is missing and the firm-month will not be ranked.

Quantile assignment is performed separately within each month and uses a three-bin split; if too few distinct values exist, fewer bins may be formed and some labels may be missing. The override to 0 applies only when the computed predicted yield equals exactly zero; negative yields are excluded from ranking but are not explicitly set to 0.

All inputs are aligned on a monthly timestamp derived from the ex-distribution date for distributions and the provided month timestamp for monthly data. The signal for a given month uses only information merged into that same month record, with the forecast implemented via lagged dividend amounts.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract: The output is a monthly firm-level signal stored as an integer year-month key paired with the firm identifier. The signal field takes values in $\{0,1,2,3\}$, where 1–3 are month-specific terciles among strictly positive predicted yields and 0 indicates exactly zero predicted yield. Firm-months without an assigned signal are omitted from the output.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: The distribution classification codes are used only to filter to a target distribution type and to infer a payment frequency class that determines the lag used for forecasting. The monthly return and ex-dividend return fields are merged but do not enter the computations described above.

factor_logic_in_paper.factor_name: Investment in property, plant, equipment, and inventory scaled by lagged total assets
factor_logic_in_paper.purpose: This factor measures a firm’s investment intensity by combining the year-over-year change in gross property, plant, and equipment with the year-over-year change in total inventories, then scaling the sum by total assets from twelve months earlier. The intent is to capture balance-sheet investment activity in tangible capital and working capital relative to firm size.
factor_logic_in_paper.inputs: The computation uses firm identifier, security identifier, and a monthly availability timestamp to align observations over time. It requires gross property, plant, and equipment; total inventories; and total assets, each expressed as balance-sheet stock values. It also relies on the same three balance-sheet items lagged by twelve months for the same security.
factor_logic_in_paper.computation_logic:
Start from the monthly panel of firm observations containing identifiers, the monthly availability timestamp, and the three balance-sheet items. Keep only these required fields for the calculation.

Remove duplicate observations for the same security and month, retaining the first occurrence. Then sort observations by security and the monthly availability timestamp to ensure correct time ordering.

Within each security’s time series, compute twelve-month lagged values for gross property, plant, and equipment; total inventories; and total assets. These lags are taken as the value from exactly twelve monthly steps earlier.

Compute the year-over-year change in gross property, plant, and equipment as the current value minus its twelve-month lag. Compute the year-over-year change in total inventories as the current value minus its twelve-month lag.

Compute the investment signal as the sum of the two year-over-year changes divided by lagged total assets. If lagged total assets equals zero, set the signal to missing rather than dividing.
factor_logic_in_paper.formulas:
Let $P_t$ be gross property, plant, and equipment at month $t$, $I_t$ be total inventories at month $t$, and $A_t$ be total assets at month $t$. Let $P_{t-12}$, $I_{t-12}$, and $A_{t-12}$ denote the corresponding values lagged by twelve months.

The intermediate changes are:
$$
\Delta P_t = P_t - P_{t-12}
$$
$$
\Delta I_t = I_t - I_{t-12}
$$

The factor value is:
$$
\text{InvestPPEInv}_t =
\begin{cases}
\frac{\Delta P_t + \Delta I_t}{A_{t-12}}, & \text{if } A_{t-12} \neq 0 \\
\text{missing}, & \text{if } A_{t-12} = 0
\end{cases}
$$
factor_logic_in_paper.edge_cases_and_timing:
If a security lacks at least twelve prior monthly observations, the twelve-month lags are missing, which makes the factor missing for that month. If any of the required current or lagged balance-sheet items are missing, the corresponding change and the final factor value become missing.

If lagged total assets is exactly zero, the factor is set to missing to avoid division by zero. Duplicate security-month records are resolved by keeping the first record encountered before lagging and differencing.

The timing uses the monthly availability timestamp as the ordering key, and the lag is defined as twelve monthly steps in that ordered series. This is a mechanical twelve-step lag and does not attempt to infer fiscal-year alignment beyond the provided monthly panel.
factor_logic_in_paper.output_contract:
The output is a monthly predictor value per security-month observation after de-duplication. The value is a dimensionless ratio equal to combined year-over-year changes in two balance-sheet stocks scaled by lagged total assets.

The output is missing when the twelve-month lag is unavailable, when required inputs are missing, or when lagged total assets equals zero. The output is intended to be saved as a named predictor series corresponding to this factor.
factor_logic_in_paper.appendix: Gross property, plant, and equipment is the total gross book value of tangible fixed assets before accumulated depreciation. Total inventories include raw materials, work in process, and finished goods, and may vary in comparability due to valuation methods. Total assets reflect reported balance-sheet totals and can be affected by restatements and acquisition accounting, which may influence year-over-year changes.
